Kocaeli Çocuk Evleri Sitesi Müdürlüğü'nde kalan 14-17 yaşlarındaki 10 kız çocuğu, 3 görevli personelle birlikte günübirlik gezi için Bolu Yedigöller ve Gölcük Tabiat Parkı'na gitti. Ancak saat 16.30'dan itibaren servis aracıyla iletişim kesildi.
Saat 19.10 sıralarında durumun Bolu AFAD'a bildirilmesi üzerine bölgede geniş çaplı arama kurtarma operasyonu başlatıldı. Son GPS sinyalinin Yedigöller'deki Kapankaya Seyir Terası mevkisinden alınması üzerine jandarma, AFAD, sağlık ve UMKE ekipleri harekete geçti.
Düzce ve Kocaeli'den gelen ekiplerin de destek verdiği çalışmalara 178 personel ve 48 araç katıldı. Ormanlık ve engebeli arazide karadan aramalar sürdürülürken dronlar ve insansız hava araçları da kullanıldı.
Saatler süren çalışmaların ardından beklenen haber geldi. Kayıp servis aracının Düzce'nin Yığılca ilçesinde bataklığa saplandığı tespit edildi.
Aile ve Sosyal Hizmetler Bakanı Mahinur Özdemir Göktaş, Bolu İl Jandarma Komutanlığı'nda yaptığı açıklamada 10 çocuk ile 3 görevlinin tamamına ulaşıldığını ve sağlık durumlarının iyi olduğunu duyurdu.
Göktaş, arama kurtarma çalışmalarına katılan ekiplere ve destek veren vatandaşlara teşekkür ederek, çocukların kısa süre içerisinde sağlık kontrolünden geçirileceğini belirtti.
Bakan Göktaş, çocukların ve görevli personelin araçta mahsur kaldıkları süre boyunca yaşadıklarını şu sözlerle anlattı:
"Bataklığa saplanınca hepsi aslında biraz çabalamış. İtmeye çalışmışlar, ayakkabıları zaten çamur içerisindeydi, çorapları da ıslanmasın diye poşet bağlamışlar. Bu bizi çok duygulandırdı. Çocukların gayreti, azmi var. Aynı zamanda bakım personelimiz çok tecrübeli, özellikle akünün bitmemesi için çaba sarf etmişler, bizi görürler, ışıkların hepsini şimdi açmayalım, seslenmişler, epeyce çaba sarf etmişler. Belki aracı itersek çıkarırız diye bakmışlar. Biraz etrafa bakınmışlar ama akşam çok hızlı karanlık çökünce ışığın olmadığı bir yerde biraz endişeli bir süreç olmuş. Şuna da sevindim 'Devletimiz bizi arıyordur.' duygusundan hiç şüphe duymamışlar. 'Bizi görecekler, bizi bulacaklar.' ama tabii çok korkmuşlar. Biz de onlar kadar korktuk. Gerçekten çok endişeli saatler geçirdik."
İçişleri Bakanı Mustafa Çiftçi de arama çalışmalarına ilişkin bilgi verdi. Çiftçi, servis aracının orman yolunda kaybolduğunu ve bataklığa saplandığını, bölgede telefonların çekmemesi nedeniyle araçtakilerin herhangi bir yere haber veremediğini açıkladı.
İletişimin sağlanabilmesi için bölgeye 11 mobil baz istasyonu yönlendirildi. Sinyallerin güçlendirilmesinin ardından araçtaki personelle telefon üzerinden bağlantı kurulabildi.
Kurtarılan 10 kız çocuğu ve 3 görevli, Bolu İl Jandarma Komutanlığı'na getirildi. Burada çocukları Bakan Göktaş karşıladı. İlk kontrollerinin ardından çocuklar ve görevli personel Kocaeli'ye gönderildi. Servis aracının sürücüsünün ise ifadesine başvuruldu.
Saatler süren belirsizlik, 13 kişinin de sağ salim bulunmasıyla sona erdi.

İstanbul Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığı, sosyal medya platformu X'in şikâyeti üzerine siber saldırı soruşturması başlattı. Soruşturma kapsamında 4 şüpheli gözaltına alındı. Şüphelilerin Türkiye üzerinden kurdukları bilişim sistemleriyle ABD 'li siyasetçilerin, şirketlerin ve bir Türk milletvekilinin hesaplarını hedef aldığı öne sürüldü.
Soruşturma, X Corp.'un altyapısına ve sunucularına yönelik siber saldırı iddialarıyla ilgili yapılan şikâyet üzerine başlatıldı. İstanbul Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığı Bilişim Suçları Soruşturma Bürosu tarafından yürütülen çalışmada 4 kişi hakkında gözaltı kararı verildi.
Şüphelilerin ikamet adreslerinde arama ve el koyma işlemi gerçekleştirildi. Aramalarda suç unsuru içerdiği değerlendirilen dijital materyallere el konuldu. Başsavcılığın açıklamasında gözaltına alınanların kimlikleri paylaşılmadı.
Açıklamaya göre şüpheliler, Türkiye'de kurdukları bilişim sistemleri üzerinden hareket etti.
Başsavcılığın aktardığına göre şüpheliler, ABD 'deki siyasi liderlerin, şirket yöneticilerinin, markaların ve haber kuruluşlarının hesaplarını hedef aldı. Listede görevdeki Kongre üyeleri, kolluk kuvvetlerine ait hesaplar, gri rozetli hükümet hesapları ve ticari ortakların hesapları da yer aldı. X'te gri rozet, genellikle hükümet ve resmi kurum hesaplarını işaret ediyor.
Ele geçirilen hesaplar arasında ABD Başkanı Donald Trump 'ın kabine üyelerinin hesaplarının yanı sıra TBMM 'de görevli bir milletvekilinin hesabının da bulunduğu öne sürüldü.

Türkiye’de dört kişi sosyal medya platformu X’e siber saldırı düzenledikleri iddiasıyla gözaltına alındı. Şüphelilerin ABD’li siyasetçiler, şirketler ve bir Türk milletvekiline ait hesapları hedef aldığı iddia ediliyor.
İstanbul başsavcılığının açıklamasına göre X Corp. ‘un şikayeti üzerine yürütülen soruşturmada bazı şüphelilerin Türkiye’den kurdukları bilişim sistemiyle platformun altyapısı ve sunucularına saldırdıkları belirlendi.
Başsavcılığın açıklamasına şüphelilerin şunların hesabını ele geçirdiği öne sürülüyor:
Son dönemde ABD ve Avrupa çeşitli alanlarda siber saldırılara maruz kalıyor.
Avrupa Birliği’nde (AB) şimdiye kadar süpermarketlerin soğutma sistemleri, bankacılık sistemi ve bazı kurumlar siber saldırılarla hedef alındı.
Birlik, siber güvenlik için 16 Ocak 2023’te NIS2 Direktifi’ni (Ağ ve Bilgi Güvenliği Direktifi 2) yürürlüğe sokmuştu. Avrupa Komisyonu 27 üye ülkeye yasalarını direktifle uyumlu hale getirmesi için 17 Ekim 2024’e kadar süre vermiş, ‘gereğini yapmayan’ 23 ülkeye ihtar göndermişti.
Komisyon daha sonra 19 ülkenin süreci başarıyla tamamladığını belirterek uyum sürecini tamamlamadığını tespit ettiği İspanya, Fransa, İrlanda ve Hollanda’yı AB Adalet Divanı’na sevk etmişti.
Komisyonun Teknolojik Egemenlik, Güvenlik ve Demokrasiden Sorumlu Başkan Yardımcısı Henna Virkkunen, 11 Kasım’da “Son günlerdeki bazı siber saldırılar AB kuralları etkin şekilde uygulansaydı önlenebilirdi” dedi.
ABD’yse hava ulaşımı, bankacılık ve ulusal güvenlik sistemlerini etkileyen siber saldırılara maruz kaldı.
Başkan Donald Trump siber saldırıların ardından Beyaz Saray Ulusal Siber Güvenlik Direktörü Sean Cairncross’u görevden aldı.
ABD Federal Soruşturma Bürosu’ysa (FBI) hackerların dünyada siber saldırıları otonomlaştırmak amacıyla yapay zeka destekli bir araç kullandığını duyurdu .

İstanbul Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığı Bilişim Suçları Soruşturma Bürosu tarafından X Corp.'un şikayeti üzerine yürütülen soruşturma kapsamında, bazı şüphelilerin Türkiye üzerinden kurdukları bilişim sistemleri ile X Corp.'un altyapısına ve sunucularına yönelik saldırı yaptıkları belirlendi.
Soruşturma kapsamında, ABD'de bulunan siyasi liderler, üst yöneticiler, şirketler, markalar, haber ağları, görevdeki ABD kongre üyeleri, kolluk kuvvetleri ve gri rozetli hükümet hesapları, ticari ortaklar ve ABD Başkanı Donald Trump'ın kabine üyeleri ile TBMM'de görevli bir milletvekilinin hesaplarının ele geçirildiği iddialarına yönelik araştırma yapıldı.

ABD ordusu, Hava Kuvvetlerinin başlıca bulut bilişim platformuna sızıldığı yönündeki haberlerin ardından cuma günü sistemlerinin güvenli olduğunu açıkladı.
Bir Pentagon yetkilisi, "Savaş Bakanlığının sistemleri güvenli, koruma altında ve dünyanın en iyi uzmanlarıyla ekipleri tarafından 7 gün 24 saat yönetiliyor. Görev açısından kritik tüm operasyon ve uygulamaların devamlılığını sağlayacağız," dedi.
Cuma günü daha önce açıklama yapan bir yetkili ise "Savaş Bakanlığı, kurumsal politikası ve operasyon güvenliği gereği ağlarının durumuna ilişkin yorum yapmaz," ifadelerini kullanmıştı.
Pentagon, Hava Kuvvetlerinin Cloud One platformuna sızılıp sızılmadığı sorusuna doğrudan yanıt vermedi. Reuters'a konuşan kaynaklar ise Cloud One'daki güvenlik ihlalinin son bir ay içinde tespit edildiğini söyledi.
Reuters'ın aktardığı kaynaklara göre çok sayıda hassas taktik, kişisel ve lojistik veriyi riske atabilecek güvenlik ihlali, platform genelinde aksamalara yol açtı.
Kaynaklar, "Bu platforma sızılması çok ciddi bir mesele," değerlendirmesinde bulundu.
Reuters'a göre ABD Hava Kuvvetlerinin bulut tabanlı komuta ve kontrol platformu; hava savunma radarları, Kuzey Amerika genelinden gelen veri akışları ve dünya çapındaki 200'den fazla Hava Kuvvetleri noktasında bomba ve füzeleri takip eden muharebe sistemleri için kullanılıyor.
NBC News, cuma günü bulut platformuna sızıldığını ve saldırının "hassas askerî bilgileri açığa çıkarmış olabileceğini" bildirdi. ABD federal kurumlarına ilişkin haberler yayımlayan Federal News Network de olay hakkında bilgi sahibi bir kaynağa dayanarak güvenlik ihlalini haberleştirdi.
Cloud One uzun süredir bilgisayar korsanlarının hedefinde. Platformun yöneticileri, 2023 yılında sızma girişimlerini engellemede "yüzde 100 başarı oranı" sağladıklarını söylemişti.
Son haftalarda ABD Merkezi İstihbarat Teşkilatı (CIA) ve Federal Soruşturma Bürosunun (FBI) da siber saldırılara hedef olduğu bildirildi. JPMorgan Chase, Visa ve Mastercard gibi büyük Amerikan finans kuruluşlarının tedarikçilerinin de saldırıya uğradığı öne sürüldü.
Microsoft Outlook, ABD'nin hava trafik kontrol sistemleri ve Ulusal Güvenlik Ajansına (NSA) ait çok gizli bir ağda da yakın dönemde sorunlar yaşandı. Yetkililer, bu kesintilerin sistemlere sızılmasından değil, bakım çalışmaları veya arızalardan kaynaklandığını vurguladı.
Benzer olaylar ABD'yle sınırlı değil. Avrupa Komisyonu da ekim ayında yapay zekâ destekli bir siber saldırıya uğramıştı.

Aile ve Sosyal Hizmetler Bakanlığı, Kocaeli Çocuk Evleri Sitesi Müdürlüğünde kalan 14-17 yaş aralığındaki 10 kız çocuğu ve 3 görevli personelin katılımıyla Bolu Yedigöller ve Gölcük Tabiat Parkı'na günübirlik gezi düzenlendiğini açıkladı. Gezi dönüşünde araçla irtibatın kesilmesi üzerine ilgili kurumlara bilgi verildi ve bölgeye arama kurtarma ekipleri sevk edildi.
Aile ve Sosyal Hizmetler Bakanlığı, Bolu Yedigöller bölgesinde haber alınamayan araç için AFAD, Jandarma ve Bakanlık ekipleri tarafından arama ve inceleme çalışmalarının sürdüğünü açıkladı.
Aile ve Sosyal Hizmetler Bakanlığı sanal medya hesabından yapılan açıklamada şöyle denildi:
“Bolu Yedigöller bölgesine gezi amacıyla giden, çocukları taşıyan araca ulaşılamaması üzerine aşağıdaki açıklamanın yapılması gereği duyulmuştur. Kocaeli Çocuk Evleri Sitesi Müdürlüğümüzde bulunan 14-17 yaş aralığındaki 10 kız çocuğumuz ve 3 görevli personelimizin katılımıyla Bolu Yedigöller Gölcük Tabiat Parkı'na günübirlik gezi düzenlenmiştir. Ve gezi dönüşünde araçla irtibatın kesilmesi üzerine ilgili kurumlara bilgi verilmiş ve bölgeye arama kurtarma ekipleri sevk edilmiştir. Çocuklarımıza ve görevli personelimize en kısa sürede ulaşılması amacıyla AFAD, Jandarma ve Bakanlık ekiplerimiz tarafından arama ve inceleme çalışmaları ayrıca dron destekli şekilde titizlikle sürdürülmektedir. Bakanlığımız, arama kurtarma çalışmalarını ilgili kurumlarla koordinasyon içerisinde yakından takip etmektedir.”
Bolu Yedigöller bölgesinde kaybolan çocuklar ve personel için arama kurtarma çalışmalarının koordinasyonu için Bolu Jandarma Komutanlığı'nda bir kriz masası oluşturuldu. Bolu'ya Kocaeli, Sakarya, Düzce il AFAD ekiplerinin yönlendirildiği bildirildi. Bakan Göktaş'ın buradan çalışmaları takip ettiği belirtildi.
Ulaştırma ve altyapı bakanlığı'ndan yapılan açıklamada "Ulaştırma ve Altyapı Bakanımız Sayın Abdulkadir Uraloğlu'nun talimatı ile Bolu'da kaybolan 10 çocuk ve 3 görevlinin arama kurtarma çalışmalarına destek vermek amacıyla yakın bölgelerden Türk Telekom tarafından 8, Turkcell tarafından da 3 olmak üzere 11 mobil baz istasyonu bölgeye yönlendirildi" ifadelerine yer verildi.
Açıklamada ayrıca "Ayrıca Karayolları Genel Müdürlüğümüz tarafından ilk etapta 2 adet çift bıçaklı kamyon, 2 adet arazi aracı ile birlikte 8 personel arama kurtarma bölgesine yönlendirilmiştir" dendi.
İletişim Başkanı Burhanettin Duran, sosyal medyadan yaptığı açıklamada şu ifadelere yer verdi:
Bolu’da Yedigöller bölgesine düzenlenen gezinin dönüşünde, 10 çocuğumuzu ve 3 görevli personelimizi taşıyan araçla irtibatın kesilmesi üzerine ilgili kurumlarımız, arama kurtarma çalışmalarını koordinasyon içerisinde ve titizlikle sürdürmektedir. En büyük temennimiz, çocuklarımıza ve görevli personelimize bir an önce sağ salim ulaşılmasıdır. Bu hassas süreçte medya kuruluşlarımızın sorumlu bir yayın anlayışıyla hareket etmeleri; kamuoyunun ise resmî makamların açıklamalarını takip ederek doğruluğu teyit edilmemiş bilgilere itibar etmemesi büyük önem taşımaktadır.
Aile ve Sosyal Hizmetler Bakanı Mahinur Özdemir Göktaş Bolu İl Jandarma Komutanlığı'na geldi. Son bilgileri paylaşan Bakan Göktaş "10 kız çocuğumuz ve 3 görevli personelimizin bulunduğu aracın dönüş yolunda araçtaki GPS'e ulaşılamıyor. Valimiz hem bize hem de ilgili kurumlara haber verdi. Dron destekli arama çalışmaları devam ediyor. Ben de yoldayım. Alana gidiyorum. Tez zamanda çocuklarıma ulaşacağız. Dönüş yolunda aracın yoldan saptığını görüyoruz. Bölge de biraz dağlık. Devlet olarak elimizden gelen her şeyi yapıyoruz çocuklarımızı bulmak için. Olay yerinde operasyonu takip edeceğim.Bolu Yedigöller dönüş yolunda seyir terasında mola veriyorlar. 16.30 gibi sinyalizasyon kayboluyor. Araçtakilerin GPS kayıtlarına ulaşmaya çalışıyoruz. Saha da büyük bir saha. Anbean takip ediliyor. Son aldığımız sinyal üzerine arama kurtarma çalışmaları yapılıyor." dedi.
Aile ve Sosyal Hizmetler Bakanlığı AKUT Arama Kurtarma Derneği Operasyon yöneticisi Serhat Akbel, Habertürk'e yaptığı açıklamada şunları söyledi:
Bölgedeki AFAD yetkilileri askeri ve jandarma yetkilileriyle hızlı bir şekilde ekipleri bölgeye yönlendiriyoruz. Biz de bölgeden bilgi topluyoruz. Bakanlık ve AFAD yetkilileriyle iletişim halindeyiz. Çok hızlı olacak şekilde bölgeye ekipler yönlendiriliyor. Termal taramalar ve dronlarla tespit çalışası yapılıyor. Devletin resmi kurumları da buralarda çalışma yapılıyor. Aracın son görüldüğü nokta, olası rota ve planlanan rotalar köpeklerle aranıyor ve dronlarla taranıyor.
Bolu gibi ağaçlık ve engebeli alanlarda arama yapmak farklı stratejileri gerektiriyor. Şu anda çevre iller ve Bolu'nun kaynaklarından ekipler bölgeye yönlendiriliyor. Sonuçta ağaç yapısı, farklı engebelerin olması yereldeki planlamalarımızın farklılaşmasına sebep oluyor.
Doğada kayıplarla çok sık karşılaşıyoruz. Örnek vermek gerekirse mantar toplamaya çıkanlar gibi. Yedigöller bölgesi çok sıkça kampların kurulduğu, yürüyüşlerin yapıldığı rotalar. 13 kişinin kaybolması bir kişinin kaybolmasına göre çok daha avantajlı bir durum. Tek bir kişiyi aramaya çıktığınızda küçük ipuçlarından hareket ediyorsunuz. Şimdi çok daha geniş bir grubu aramamız söz konusu. Doğada kaybolmalar bizim çoklukla yaptığımız operasyonlardan biri. Ekiplerimiz bölgede teyakkuz halindeler. Tamamen AFAD koordinasyonuyla koordineliyiz. Umut ediyoruz ki kimsenin burnu bile kanamadan bir an önce evlerine ulaşmalarıdır.

Şu an itibariyle bölgeye giden yol kesildi. Vatandaşların geçişine izin verilmiyor. En son sinyal alınan yer Yedigöller Kapankaya seyir noktası. Şu anda orada iletişim sorunu var. Burada en acil iletişim sorunlarının giderilmesi gerekiyor.
Edinilen bilgilere göre Bolu Yedigöller bölgesinde 3 adet İHA sahayı tarama çalışmalarına başladı. İHA'lar bölgede 6 noktayı taradı. Çalışmalara Bayraktar insansız hava aracının da destek verdiği öğrenildi.

Şu anda Aile ve Sosyal Hizmetler Bakanı Mahinur Özdemir Göktaş çalışmaları takip ediyor. Ekipler havadan ve karadan sahada çalışmaya devam ediyor. Bu nokta son telefon sinyalinin alındığı konuma kuş uçuşu ile 1 saatlik uzaklıktı.
Aile ve Sosyal Hizmetler Bakanı Mahinur Göktaş, Düzce'nin Yığılca ilçesinde aracın bataklığa saplandığını belirterek "Çok şükür müjdeli haberi aldık. Çocuklarımız ve bütün ekip sağ. Araç bataklığa saplanmış. Durumları çok çok iyi elhamdülillah" diye konuştu.

You should never buy a TV at full price. This is a hill I will die on, and I am proven right every year when I see 20-, 30-, and even 60-percent-off Black Friday TV deals on some of the best TVs you can buy .
If you're in the market for a new screen, now is a smart time to shop options of all sizes, from big, premium OLED TVs for a home theater to small art TVs for the bedroom. One of our team of WIRED reviewers has tried every TV featured below (with one exception, the LG C6, which is currently in testing) to ensure we can stand by our recommendations.
For more great discounts, check out our guide to the Absolute Best Black Friday deals , as well as Best Tech Deals, Best Black Friday Headphone Deals , and Best Black Friday Apple Deals .
Updated November 28: I’ve added more RGB TV deals and updated the prices of every deal in this guide.
This is the lowest price I've ever seen the 65-inch LG C6 selling for on Amazon. It's a fantastic deal on an excellent OLED TV. Right now it's 48 percent off its retail price of $2,700, though I did spot it at 50 percent off yesterday (briefly). LG's C-Series TVs are consistently among our favorites due to their high brightness, uniform blacks, and vivid, natural colors. Add in their ample connectivity, which makes them versatile enough for gamers, and it's clear why this is a top OLED pick.
The premium 2026 Samsung S95H OLED TV is now at its lowest price yet. WIRED contributor John Brandon praised the TV for its accurate color and deep blacks. New to the latest S95H model is a silver bezel that’s recessed behind the main OLED panel, making the TV look like a metal picture frame.
One of our favorite budget OLED TVs, the Roku Pro Series OLED is on sale for the first time ever this Black Friday. It has Roku's easy-to-use software built in, and while it isn't the brightest OLED around, it's certainly one of the cheapest right now.
In his review of the Hisense U7SG , former WIRED reviewer Ryan Waniata called this a near-premium model with a new-and-improved stand and an anti-reflective matte screen reminiscent of high-end Samsung models. The best part? It's down an extra $50 to its lowest price ever since its launch in April of this year.
Spoiler for our upcoming review: This is one of the best midrange TVs available. It's a fantastic option that will satisfy most people, and at its current 40-percent-off price, it'll also satisfy most budgets. Like so many of the TVs on the list, this is the lowest price this model has ever dropped to. More importantly, though, WIRED reviewer Rick Broida was seriously impressed by its bright and vibrant color display, which has a distinct pop that’s a joy to behold.
The LG Micro RGB Evo takes the top spot in our guide to the best RGB TVs , and again, this is the lowest price I've ever seen for it, by a lot. WIRED contributor John Brandon thought movies and shows looked stunning and vivid on its screen, with highly customizable picture settings that put it in a league of its own. Keep in mind that it only comes in 75-, 86-, and 100-inch sizes.
The best art TV is Samsung's The Frame Pro (2026) thanks to its excellent image quality, contrast, color depth, and anti-glare technology that far outshines the competition, says Brandon. The only problem is that it's historically been high-priced. While 17 percent off may not sound that impressive, it’s actually matching the Prime Day low I saw earlier this year for the same model.
If you're set on an art TV but can't spring for Samsung's pricey options, this budget-friendly model is the way to go. At 53 percent off, it matches its October Prime Day pricing (which is the lowest it's ever been). It's not as bright as Samsung's art TVs, but it does come with a far broader free art library with no subscription required.
This is the best soundbar you can get if you want a one-and-done, all-in-one solution. The Sonos Arc Ultra earned high praise from every WIRED reviewer who has tested it (myself included) for its rich, deep, convincingly spatial sound. If you still want to upgrade, Sonos makes it easy to add other Sonos speakers , like a subwoofer or rear surrounds.
This soundbar-subwoofer combo is a great way to upgrade your TV audio system with ample bass for a low price, especially with this Black Friday deal. It's simple and easy to use, and doesn't overwhelm with additional features, options, and connectivity like some higher-end options. As long as you don't dream of creating a full surround sound system later, the S4 will serve you for years.
The Hisense XR10 is an excellent home theater projector thanks to its vivid and sharp color output in movies, TV shows, and games—it really makes everything pop. At $2,000 off, this is the biggest discount ever for the XR10. Keep in mind, this thing is heavy at 23 pounds, so it's more of a set-it-and-forget-it home projector, and, like many premium projectors, it's just OK when used in a bright, sunny room.

If the barista at your neighborhood coffee shop knows your order before you even walk up to the counter, it might be time to consider learning to make that double Americano at home. Lucky for you, there's no shortage of Black Friday espresso machine deals on a variety of options, including a basic De’Longhi selling for less than $200, an old-school machine handmade in Milan, and much more.
Each deal below is for a machine that a WIRED reviewer has tested and vetted in their own kitchen. For more savings, check out our Best Black Friday Deals .
Updated November 28, 2026: We've added new deals on machines from Flair and Bosch, and ensured up-to-date prices.
WIRED reviewers have tried and liked a couple of machines from Diletta, a line of Italian-made, classic semiautomatics exclusive to Seattle Coffee Gear, and they’re all on sale today through December 14.
When our reviewer tested the Bello+ in 2024, she appreciated the stylish, industrial design (handmade in Milan) and easily maneuverable steam wand. Though she found the machine itself to be a bit finicky, Seattle Coffee Gear claims it has a programmable pre-infusion for repeatable recipes.
Best Traditional Espresso Machine in our guide to the best , the Mio is stylish and built to last, with an analog design and a two-year warranty. It also makes for a solid first “real” espresso machine with its built-in shot timer and pressure gauge.
Fellow set some pretty lofty expectations with the release of its sleek Aiden coffee maker in 2024 , and according to former WIRED reviewer and espresso expert Matthew Korfhage , the brand didn't disappoint on its first attempt at an espresso machine. The ability to adjust flow rates and pressure curves was once the province of, as Korfhage put it, only the “richest and nerdiest of nerds.” But Fellow now allows you—yes, you, at home in your kitchen—to fine-tune how water moves through the grounds, unlocking previously unforeseen dimensions of flavor.
When we tested this machine , we liked it for a variety of reasons, including an easy-to-use milk frother and two swappable bean hoppers, which are especially helpful if you like to switch to decaf in the afternoons. It comes in a variety of finishes, but note that Beige is the cheapest of all right now, at only $915 .
This flashy, design-oriented semiautomatic (“a steampunk gasworks of a thing ,” according to Korfhage) is quite dramatic in person. It has a dual boiler—meaning you can froth milk at the same time you’re pulling a shot—and it comes with a nice set of accessories, including a tamper and milk pitcher. Note that this sale is on the second-gen machine, which features expanded grinder settings and a new portafilter.
The Best Semiautomatic Machine for Most People , the Barista Express is a longtime Reviews team favorite and platonic ideal of an espresso machine, with its pressure gauge and industrial-looking steam wand. If you want a built-in grinder without dropping four figures, this is your machine and your sale.
Formerly the Linea Classic, De’Longhi’s Classic is the best bare-bones espresso machine we’ve tried , with a pressure gauge, 15-bar pump, and updated thermoblock system. I used one for a full year and, while it’s not as foolproof as a semiautomatic, it was easy enough for morning espresso shots and cappuccinos; I even pulled off some rudimentary latte art with its steam wand.
The Vertuo Pop+ is our favorite pod maker for espresso . The Deluxe model adds a larger, side-mount water tank (37 ounces to the original’s 25 ounces) and new finishes, including this white one, a matte black-and-gold, and a sort of gunmetal gray.
OK, yes, this is not an espresso machine, but it is Korfhage's personal favorite coffee maker . “No device I know makes single-mug drip coffee this delicious with such ease and simplicity,” he writes in his review of the machine. It's perfect for just one or two people who don't need an entire carafe's worth of joe in the morning but also enjoy pour-over-style coffee and have no desire to futz with a Chemex .
When we reviewed this semiautomatic in 2024 , we appreciated its slim profile, consistent shots, and built-in burr grinder. The cold-brew setting is more of a gimmick than a way to make actual cold brew, and some design choices are a bit quirky. Even so, it’s a beautiful, industrial-looking machine that takes up only 12 inches of counter space.
Ninja sometimes has a reputation for doing too much, but this semiautomatic is a solid beginner-friendly option that pulls good shots. It’s got a built-in grinder and milk frother, the latter of which can make cold foam and even has a setting for plant-based milk. In true Ninja fashion, the machine also has settings for drip coffee and cold brew, but neither impressed our tester, so I wouldn’t buy it for those features alone.
In May of this year, WIRED’s UK team did a blind taste test of espresso made with a variety of machines, including the Terra Kaffe TK-02 (below) and this Philips Café Aromis 8000 Series. The Philips won overall for its flavorful, balanced espresso and lattes. Our US Reviews team will be testing the Philips soon for our own guide , but you can see what the fuss is all about ahead of that with this 20-percent-off deal.
Our favorite pod machine for cold brew also has an Espresso setting that dispenses 2-ounce shots of espresso-style concentrate—perfectly chilled for iced coffee drinks. This is a huge machine and a huge investment (it only takes proprietary pods that cost more than $2 apiece), but if you have much love for cold coffee drinks ( or espresso martinis ) and little time to mess with a toddy or other manual machine, it will get you top-tier results within minutes.
Whether you want consistent espresso on the go or just prefer doing things the hard way, the Flair is our favorite manual espresso machine . It's how it was done in the old days, when pulling a shot was physically pulling a shot. It's not often on sale, so if you'd been considering it for a gift or for yourself this is a rare opportunity to save 20 percent.
Look, not everyone has the time or patience for the romance and ritual of espresso making, and that's OK. A weekday morning is not often the time for fitzing and futzing, and sometimes any task beyond pushing a button is enough to push you into the Starbucks drive-thru. This Bosch model has a touchscreen with many drink options downloaded via firmware, and former WIRED reviewer Matthew Korfhage appreciated that it lets you steam milk inside the machine or in a separate container, if your family uses multiple types of milk.
Korfhage tested Terra Kaffe's newer Demi and said it was perhaps the “dead-simplest fully automatic espresso machine I've yet encountered that still makes good coffee,” with just a dial and a button. Right now it's $200 off, or $300 off with a coffee subscription (Terra-Kaffe offers a house blend specifically made for its own machines). Its bigger sibling, the TK-02, impressed our tester with its convenience, ease of use, front-facing water filter, and milk carafe. Though it didn't come out on top during an espresso blind taste test we conducted earlier this year , it's still a great-looking machine that's easy to use. It's also a whopping $400 off (or $500 with a coffee subscription) for Black Friday.
Maybe you or your recipient already has an espresso machine; in that case, they’ll need some quality beans. Our favorite coffee subscription , Atlas Coffee Club, has a new gift option on offer for Black Friday : a quarterly subscription of three bags of unique, globally sourced coffee every three months for $59 . You can choose any roast you want, including espresso roast and even Nespresso pods. If you’d rather buy an ongoing subscription for yourself, your first bag is free with Atlas’ Black Friday sale.
Former barista and WIRED contributing reviewer Pete Cottell likes this little scale that includes three magnetic add-ons: a platform, a metal dosing cup, and a catch cup that fit…

Brands have largely finished launching their latest models for the year, and I'm seeing some stellar Black Friday headphone deals on new and older headphones alike. Apple AirPods Pro 3 are the best wireless earbuds not only for anyone with an iPhone—but also for anyone who wants to keep things simple. They sound great and have some of the best active-noise-canceling (ANC) and transparency modes on the market. They also seamlessly sync with all of your Apple devices. At $100 off, it's the lowest price they've ever been at.
This is the lowest price I’ve ever seen on one of my favorite pairs of wireless earbuds. The Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro have one magic trick: call quality. To put it simply, I sound better talking on calls using these earbuds than any other I’ve tested, and it’s not a close competition. Beyond that, they’re solid all-rounders, with good noise-canceling, sound quality, and versatility.
These are our go-to earbuds of choice for anyone with a Samsung Galaxy phone thanks to great noise-canceling and transparency. The Samsung Galaxy Buds 4 Pro are their lowest price ever this Black Friday.
If you've got an Android phone, the Google Pixel Buds Pro 2 are excellent wireless earbuds that strike the rare combination of small, comfortable, and secure—great for daily life and working out alike.
Want workout earbuds that won't fall out? Get these Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 . They're some of the more secure-fitting earbuds I've ever tested. Plus, they have great noise-canceling, transparency, and even built-in heart-rate sensors, so you can track your workout even if you left your fitness tracker at home.
The Nothing Ear (3a) are one of our favorite pairs of earbuds under $100, and 30 percent off is the biggest discount I've ever seen for them so far. They have a semi-transparent design and bold colors that stand out from the crowd (particularly the yellow version). While the automated noise-canceling isn't the best, it's hard to fault them at this new low price.
My main gripe with the Bose QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen) is price. At 45 percent off (their lowest price ever), that complaint vanishes, making this a top headphone deal to shop. The headphones are exceedingly comfortable and have excellent ANC—far better than basically every other set of headphones at this new low price of $200.
The Nothing Headphone (1) are a home run in looks and sound, and they are at their lowest price ever ahead of Black Friday. They’re solid noise cancelers with a bold, transparent design on the ear cups that's somehow techy, retro, and futuristic-looking. Among their best features are the on-ear controls, namely the clicky wheel that adjusts volume and the flat rocker paddle that you can push back and forth to move to the previous track or skip ahead, respectively.
Nothing's most budget-friendly over-ear headphones, the Nothing Headphone (a) keep a lot of what we love about the Headphone (1), just at a lower price. Sure, noise-canceling and audio quality isn't quite as good, but the price is hard to beat.
Did you hear the news? Sony made a version two of their cult-classic Sony WH-1000XM4 headphones. This is the first time they are on sale, and at $200, they're one of the best deals this Black Friday. They have outstanding sound, great noise-canceling, a comfortable fit, and a convenient, folding design well-suited for travel.
The more premium XM6 and the newly revived (and cheaper) XM4C have effectively replaced the Sony WH-1000XM5 . But I am still seeing the blue colorway of these excellent headphones at the lowest price I've clocked for these older cans. When they launched in 2022, they were our top pick for over-ear headphones. They remain excellent and far outperform other options at this limited price.
Sony recently launched the WH-CN730N to replace these headphones, hence the rock-bottom price of 50 percent off. While these headphones can't compete with most specs of more premium options on this list, they're ultra-lightweight at just 192 grams. That weight plus 35 hours of battery life with ANC on is nothing to scoff at.
AirPods Max 2 are excellent over-ear headphones for Apple fans, but the $550 sticker price is frankly absurd. Thankfully, they are almost always a little bit on sale, including now. My top over-ear headphone pick, the best-in-class Sony WH-1000XM6 , is at its lowest price ever this Black Friday. These headphones are amazing across the board, with their high comfort, superior sound quality, and great noise-canceling capability.

An Alexa speaker with a screen that only shows your best photos? This is the smart display we’ve been asking for.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
I have to face facts: I’m a digital hoarder. My son graduated high school this year, and to mark the occasion, I made him a scrapbook of his 12 years of school. He loved it, but one reaction surprised me: He said he’d never seen most of these photos. Unlike my childhood — documented in photo albums sitting on shelves for anyone to browse — the photographic evidence of my son’s childhood is sitting on my phone. Cue the mom-guilt.
While a few photos are framed around our house, my phone holds thousands of pictures of my son that he’s never seen. And that just feels wrong. The solution to this — getting photos off your phone and into your home — is the pitch behind Amazon’s newest gadget, the Alexa Photo Frame, which starts at $199.99 .
Alexa is very good at curating your photos Only shows photos: no ads Semi-matte, anti-glare screen displays photos beautifully It’s a full Alexa speaker
Requires Amazon Photos; no Google Photos support Prime or Alexa Plus sub needed for Alexa curation Landscape only, no video Speakers are weak for music As expensive as an Echo Show 8
A smart digital photo frame that uses AI to surface your best photos automatically, the Frame is also an Alexa smart speaker. It seems Amazon has finally made the product its users have been asking for: a smart speaker that shows pictures — nothing more, nothing less. No rotating screen serving up a random smorgasbord of Alexa suggestions, weather, and news. No camera. And, best of all, no display ads. The only real question is, what took so long?
For years, Amazon’s Echo Show smart displays did a nice job displaying photos, but I couldn’t ever have them display only photos; there was always some rotating content showing Alexa suggestions or other cruft. In 2023, the company launched a more expensive dedicated photos edition of the Echo Show 8 , but quickly discontinued it. Then, last year, Echo Shows started regularly showing full-screen display ads for motor oil and recliners between my family photos — and I quickly banished them to little-seen corners of my home.
The Alexa Photo Frame feels a bit like Amazon’s apology to customers who just wanted a goddamn digital photo frame — albeit an expensive one. The Frame does exactly what I wanted the Shows to do with photos, without showing anything else.
One word of caution: while it only shows photos today, the Frame’s 10-inch touchscreen is functionally the same as the Echo Shows, meaning nothing is stopping Amazon from adding ads down the line — which is what happened with the Shows. For now, Amazon has said the device only shows photos and does not display ads. In my three weeks of testing, that’s all it’s shown, and it’s done a nice job thanks to its AI-powered photo curation feature.
As a dedicated photo device, the Alexa Photo Frame is great. Photos look lovely on its anti-glare 1280 x 800, 16:10 aspect ratio screen, and the AI-powered photo selection does the hard work of curating your photos.
My favorite feature is the Daily Memories collection, the Frame’s default album, which pulls up pictures from this time in past years. All week I’ve been seeing past Thanksgiving celebrations and shots of my now-teenage kids sitting on Santa’s lap as toddlers. It’s been genuinely delightful.
The catch is you have to use Amazon Photos. Unlike other smart frames, it has no option to import directly from Google Photos or Apple’s iCloud, where your photos most likely live. If you pay for Amazon Prime, though, Amazon Photos offers free unlimited storage, and I could import my iPhone’s photo library just by opening the app and turning on automatic backup. It took a little over a day to back up my 100,000-plus photo library.
When the Frame shows vertical images, instead of cropping them or adding black bars as some frames do, it uses AI to pair them with similar pictures: my daughter Rollerblading alongside my son playing tennis; my daughter on the beach next to a shot of her playing in the snow; my son cuddling our dog next to one of him snuggling with our cat. It does a good job of pairing similar images, and I especially like when it serves up then-and-now pictures; it’s fun to see baby pictures next to shots of my grown-up kids.
Amazon says Alexa uses a combination of faces, time, and context to sort photos for you. It looks for smiles and good lighting while skipping screenshots and receipts, and also that close-up of the mole on your shoulder. Daily Memories is my favorite, but you can choose from auto-updating collections of specific people (not pets, sadly), create albums with specific images, and have multiple collections rotating at once. You can also invite family and friends to add their photos to the Frame.
The Frame is an Alexa smart speaker, and the on-board voice assistant can answer questions about your photos. When a picture of my kids in face masks visiting Santa popped up, I asked Alexa what year it was, and it answered correctly: “2021.” Then I asked to see more photos from that day, and it pulled up all the images from our visit and a slideshow play button — this would be a neat way to show off your holiday snaps when friends visit. You can also ask it for more specific requests: “Show me all the photos of my son playing tennis” or “Show me all the photos of my daughter playing bass.”
Digital photo frames I’ve used from Aura and Skylight rely more heavily on you fiddling with an app to add new pictures. Amazon’s special sauce is that once set up, it’s largely hands-free. Of course, Google has done this with its Nest Hub smart displays for years, and they have long been my favorite digital photo frames . But Nest Hub’s hardware is aging, and its algorithms aren’t as good (I have definitely seen some mole shots). The Alexa Photo Frame’s semi-matte screen also displays photos better with less glare. However, the Frame’s screen isn’t as good as the $229 Aura Aspen, with its higher 1600 x 1200 resolution and clever 4:3 aspect ratio that displays both horizontal and portrait images beautifully.
Along with the Frame’s white mat and actual frame (in black or wood), it looks more like a photo frame and less like a piece of tech than an Echo Show or Nest Hub. Don’t get me wrong: The Frame is unmistakably a screen, but like all digital photo frames, its benefit over a regular photo frame is fresh images every few seconds, minutes, hours, or once a day.
I tested the walnut model, which costs an extra $30; there’s also a birch model and the cheaper black option. It’s very solid and well-made. A light sensor adjusts the display based on ambient light (with the option to shut it off completely in a dark room). It has four microphones and a pair of stereo speakers for Alexa, plus a physical mute button to turn the voice assistant off and volume buttons. Unlike Aura or Skylight frames, it doesn’t play video or Live Photos, only static images, but it has a unique feature that lets you add a voice note to a photo that plays when you tap on it. I didn’t find much use for this personally, but Amazon bills this as a gifting feature, since it can play a message when the recipient sets it up. Probably a good option for the grandparents.
The other feature the Frame has over the competition is that it is a full-fledged Alexa Plus speaker and can do everything an Echo Dot can, including controlling your smart home, setting timers and alarms, and booking you a table at a local restaurant. Unlike an Echo Show, it doesn’t use its display to show information, just photos. The Frame’s built-in speaker is fine for podcasts and radio — a step up from your iPhone speakers, but not a big one. For music, pairing it with an Echo or a Bluetooth speaker in the Alexa app is the way to go.
If it could display a clock over the photos, like Apple’s HomeView smart display,…

Sakana AI , a Japanese AI startup, last month revealed plans to develop its own foundation model. The move has drawn attention for its potential impact on Japan’s defense and cybersecurity sectors as well as concerns about reliance on U.S. and Chinese technologies.
Sakana AI’s co-founder and CEO, David Ha, told TechCrunch that its upcoming foundation model, Sawara, is part of the company’s broader goal of supporting and strengthening Japan’s industrial and manufacturing sectors using AI. In addition, Ha noted rising cybersecurity threats and stressed the need for domestic AI alternatives for sensitive applications, particularly if access to foreign models becomes limited.
“When we started planning for this model, of course, we had physical AI, manufacturing, and industry in mind, and we still do. This is our long-term vision,” Ha said. “But short-term, I think Japan has a real need for security-related capabilities as well.”
Sakana will begin working on Sawara this month, aiming to train and release a smaller-scale model in early 2027, followed by a larger version.
The project comes roughly five months after Sakana launched Fugu, an AI orchestration system that ropes in other large language models, including those developed by U.S. AI labs, to assemble AI agents according to the task at hand. The Tokyo-based startup has also built Namazu, a Japanese-focused language model that fine-tunes existing open-weight models from Meta and DeepSeek to better understand Japanese language, culture, and business needs, including translation, political questions, and AI agent tasks.
“We cannot simply use open-weight models as-is in Japan for enterprises because they’re usually biased towards their creators,” Ha said. “They may refuse to answer questions about Japan or Japanese politics […] they may give Japanese people answers they don’t want to hear.”
However, Ha acknowledged that developing a domestic foundation model alone will not fully eliminate reliance on foreign AI technology.
“The only thing [left] for us to become a full-stack company is the pre-training, Sawara,” Ha continued. “We plan to apply the [Sawara] technology in industry and manufacturing. We’ll train both a small and a large model next year. The small model should be particularly useful for on-premises solutions. Japan needs on-premises deployment capabilities.”
While Fugu incorporates OpenAI’s models, Ha noted that foreign AI models are not enough for certain applications. For example, in cybersecurity, Japan requires that customized models be deployed on-premises.
“Japan will continue to use U.S. systems, but it also wants domestic alternatives,” Ha said. “People often point to Palantir and other systems. I have a great deal of respect for companies such as Snowflake, Palantir, and Datadog. But for national defense, Japan will want its own systems.”
Sakana signed a research contract with Japan’s Ministry of Defense in July to explore how AI could help analyze and integrate information from multiple sources, and it has also worked with the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications , on systems for detecting disinformation.
Sakana’s work with Japanese government agencies has shaped its approach to developing Sawara, Ha said. Unlike commercial customers, government agencies often have stricter requirements, including the ability to audit training data, customize AI models and deploy them on-premises.
“Those lessons helped us plan how to develop and deploy Sawara. I think similar requirements exist in many governments,” he said.
While enterprise customers can use a combination of Fugu, Namazu and AI models developed overseas, Sakana’s government-related work currently focuses on two main areas: disinformation detection and analysis, and multimodal systems that integrate data from different government sources.
Sakana’s expansion into developing its own foundation models comes amid speculation about a potential IPO following reports by Nikkei and Bloomberg earlier this month.
But Ha said the company doesn’t have any near-term plans to go public.
The reported timing and potential valuation were speculative, Ha said, adding that he did not know when the company might pursue a listing, though he expects his startup to eventually go public in Japan itself.
“We have a gravitational pull to eventually IPO in Japan,” Ha said.
Ha sees Sakana’s future growth tied to the global expansion of Japanese manufacturers. Rather than focusing on selling its models, the company wants to help local companies use AI to become more competitive globally.
“We want to strategically work with the government and Japanese industrial base, make them competitive,” Ha said. “We want to go abroad, go international together with manufacturing and industrial sectors.”

NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has concluded its scientific mission , which spanned just under 22 years. As its orbital altitude fell below 275 kilometers (171 miles), it could no longer continue stable astronomical observations, and it reentered the atmosphere on November 4 over North Sumatra, Indonesia.
Swift had been launched on November 20, 2004, as the Swift Gamma-Ray Burst Explorer, and it began operations the following month. In addition to a gamma-ray-burst alert telescope, it was equipped with ultraviolet and visible-light telescopes as well as an x-ray telescope, and was designed as a multi-wavelength observation satellite capable of rapidly pinpointing the locations of gamma-ray bursts—the most powerful explosions in the universe. In 2018, following the death of its first principal investigator, Neil Gehrels, NASA renamed the mission in his honor.
The development of the Swift space telescope was driven by the difficulty of tracking gamma-ray bursts. “Swift was designed as a satellite dedicated to studying gamma-ray bursts, outbursts that came and went so quickly that no one could target them with large telescopes to learn more,” explains S. Bradley Cenko, the mission’s principal investigator at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center.
Swift detected a gamma-ray burst, pinpointed its location, relayed the information to other observatories, and then swiveled its telescope to capture images before the afterglow faded; this sequence of operations was usually finished in about a minute. Speed was particularly critical for short gamma-ray bursts, in which the emissions end in less than two seconds. Before Swift was launched, it was not possible to pinpoint the location quickly and accurately enough to observe the afterglow.
In May 2005, Swift quickly turned toward the gamma-ray burst GRB 050509B, which lasted only 0.03 second, and detected 11 x-ray photons. This was the first short gamma-ray burst for which an afterglow was detected. This observation corroborated long-standing theoretical models suggesting that short bursts are most likely caused by the merger of two neutron stars, celestial bodies with a mass comparable to the sun compressed to the size of a city.
Its flexible observation planning system is another reason why Swift was regarded as a versatile tool for astronomy. This is because astronomers could request target-of-opportunity observations, which allowed commands to be sent from the ground in as little as a few minutes.
It also allowed for the setup of monitoring programs to observe specific celestial objects for periods ranging from minutes to months, and it was possible to schedule observations of up to 75 distinct celestial objects per day. Furthermore, it played a role in sending alerts to other space- and ground-based facilities to coordinate additional observations.
Swift observed more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts and more than 1,400 supernova explosions. It also witnessed stars being torn apart by black holes, monitored active galaxies, and conducted all-sky x-ray surveys; the data from these observations contributed to approximately 7,000 scientific papers. The entire dataset—including approximately 22 years’ worth of brightness measurements and more than 1.5 million images from ultraviolet and visible-light telescopes— is publicly available and amounts to about 12 terabytes.
The Swift observatory was circling in low Earth orbit. At this altitude even the outermost layer of the atmosphere creates air resistance on satellites. However, Swift lacked thrusters to maintain its orbit, and its altitude continued to drop.
As a result, its altitude—which was approximately 585 kilometers (364 miles) at launch—had dropped to about 363 kilometers as of June 18, 2026. In recent years, increased solar activity has caused Earth’s atmosphere to expand, causing the telescope to descend faster than initially predicted.
NASA engineers had long predicted that Swift’s altitude would drop to approximately 300 kilometers by the fall of 2026, at which point a recovery spacecraft would no longer be able to approach it safely. Consequently, NASA decided not to issue a standard request for proposals and instead asked three companies with which it had already signed technology development contracts to explore the feasibility of providing orbital services. In September 2025, NASA signed a $30 million contract with the space startup Katalyst Space Technologies.
The Swift Space Telescope upon its completion in September 2003. Pictured alongside it is Neil Gehrels, the project’s first principal investigator. (NASA)
The original plan was for the small satellite LINK to capture and dock with Swift using three robotic arms, raise its orbit to a safe operational altitude, and resume scientific observations. Since there was only one year to complete this task, Katalyst manufactured components in-house when suppliers could not meet their deadlines and streamlined testing procedures. LINK was launched on July 3, 2026, aboard a Northrop Grumman Pegasus XL rocket.
However, during in-orbit testing, a malfunction occurred in LINK’s attitude-control system, and it was determined that capturing Swift and raising its orbit would be difficult. In response, NASA and Katalyst announced on August 19 that the operation would be canceled, and the mission was redefined as an in-orbit demonstration.
LINK raised its orbit to align with Swift, deployed its three robotic arms, and simultaneously fired its three ion thrusters, successfully approaching the telescope to a distance of 12 to 15 kilometers (7 to 9 miles). Nevertheless, NASA announced that LINK would not approach Swift any closer during the remainder of its operational life in orbit. LINK subsequently reentered Earth’s atmosphere on September 25.
Following the decision to abandon the orbital raise, the Swift operations team announced a plan to continue observations for as long as possible in the time left. On August 26, they restarted the ultraviolet- and visible-light telescopes and the x-ray telescope—which had been shut down in preparation for the rescue mission—and successfully captured images of Tycho’s supernova remnant, located approximately 13,000 light-years away. But as the altitude dropped below 275 kilometers, the telescope was no longer able to maintain a stable lock on its target, and the scientific mission concluded with the final observation on October 20.
“Swift delivered an incredible, lasting return on investment for the nation, designed for a two-year primary mission but productive for more than 10 times as long,” said Sean Domagall-Goldman, director of the Astrophysics Division at NASA headquarters. To ensure it can continue to respond swiftly to cosmic phenomena even after Swift is gone, NASA is considering ways to utilize and expand its existing fleet of space telescopes.
This story was originally published in WIRED Japan and has been translated from Japanese.

SpaceX is seeking approval to launch a million satellites into orbit to build AI data centers in space. Experts are skeptical, citing many unanswered questions. At the top of the list: Who owns the sky?
Elon Musk's space company SpaceX has got the green light from the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to build a network of 1 million satellites designed to host AI data centers in space. The project is called "Starmind."
Official approval comes with an ambitious timeline: SpaceX must have 10%, or 100,000, of the authorized satellites in orbit by 2035. By 2038, that figure must reach 50%. Within 15 years, a total of 1 million satellites are expected to orbit Earth, helping meet the rapidly growing demand for artificial intelligence computing power.
"Putting data centers onto satellites and into space is somewhat attractive due to the higher availability of solar energy," Ulrich Speidel of the University of Auckland's School of Computer Science in New Zealand told the Science Media Center.
Depending on a satellite's orbit, it would be exposed to sunlight for more than half the day, Speidel said. And, of course, there are no clouds in space.
SpaceX makes a similar argument, saying its satellites would take advantage of space's plentiful energy and cooling possibilities, reducing the burden on Earth.
Electricity consumption by AI data centers is indeed rising worldwide. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA) , their consumption could more than double to 945 terawatt-hours per year by 2030.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
In addition to electricity, data centers on Earth consume large amounts of water to cool their servers. According to a recent study, global water consumption for this purpose ranges from 313 billion to 764 billion liters (82.7 billion to 201.8 billion gallons). Around a quarter of all data centers are also located in regions that regularly experience water shortages, the study's authors said.
Cooling in space , however, is difficult, Ulrich Speidel said. "The only way to remove heat from a satellite in a vacuum is to radiate it away, rather than dissipate it as we can do here on Earth using water or air cooling."
Richard Easther, a physicist at the University of Auckland, also sees cooling as a challenge, "but there are plausible solutions that are entirely consistent with basic physics."
However, Easther told the Science Media Center that the "Starmind" project is "at the very edge of technical feasibility." He also pointed out that Elon Musk's Starlink project would have sounded far-fetched 15 years ago.
Easther said he sees the FCC timeline as unrealistic, joining others who doubt that SpaceX can meet its commitments to the agency.
"That would mean launching about eight satellites per hour from now until their deadline to complete the authorized constellation of Nov. 25, 2040," Laura Revell, a professor of atmospheric chemistry at the University of Canterbury in Christchurch, New Zealand, told the Science Media Center.
"I am extremely concerned about the levels of pollution that would accumulate in the atmosphere. We already know that emissions from rocket launches can cause depletion of the protective ozone layer," Revell said.
So far, this has not been a major problem because of the relatively small number of rocket launches. But this project could undo "decades of efforts to protect the ozone layer," she said.
The satellites themselves also pose an environmental risk, Revell said. Satellites are typically decommissioned after five years. When they reenter the atmosphere, they burn up, which "fundamentally turns the atmosphere into a crematorium for satellites," she said.
Overall, the long-term effects of vaporized metals on the atmosphere's climate and the ozone layer are entirely unknown.
Space debris is already a problem. The Starmind project would increase the number of active satellites in orbit by more than 50-fold, Michael Brown, an astronomer at Monash University in Melbourne, Australia, told the Science Media Center.
"This greatly increases the risk of collisions with space junk, which could lead to the Kessler syndrome — a cascade of collisions that would make low Earth orbit unusable."
Earth's increasingly crowded orbit is not the only factor that could make space research more difficult for astronomers in the future.
The Starmind satellites will come equipped with enormous solar panels. These will be larger and heavier than other satellites because of the cooling systems they need. This could have "devastating effects on numerous astronomical observations," physicist Richard Easther said. Even for people who are not astronomers, the view of the night sky could change dramatically.
The FCC made a decision with global implications on its own, dismissing environmental concerns as being "outside its purview," Laura Revell said.
"The question is, who has the authority to protect the upper atmosphere from rocket and satellite pollution for the common good?"
One thing is certain: Protecting the atmosphere should not be left to a company focused on maximizing profits.

If you've been using the Fitbit app in recent years, you'll know that it's now been replaced by Google Health. (Google bought Fitbit back in 2019 .) The app will eventually replace Google Fit too, though we don't know exactly when that will be. Google has previously said it will happen before the end of the year .
While many features have been carried over into Google Health from its predecessors, some haven't. There have also been new additions, and a lot of rearranging has gone on too, so it can take a while to figure out exactly where everything is.
Whether you're a veteran from the Google Fit or Fitbit days, or you've just installed Google Health for the first time to use with a new device, these tips will help you explore everything the app has to offer and get the most out of it.
If you've been waiting to buy a device to track your steps before installing Google Health, you don't have to. You can still get the step-tracking features from the app, as long as you carry your phone with you on all your walks and runs.
Tap the Connections icon (top left), then Phone to start pulling in data from your Android or iOS smartphone. If you later add a wearable, you can switch to this for steps—or keep them both enabled (handy if you forget your tracker at home one day, for example).
The Today page is the first one you see when you open the Google Health app, so it makes sense to fill it with the stats that actually matter to you, rather than the metrics the app picks. Tap the pen icon just underneath the top bank of widgets to make changes.
You're able to switch between Standard view and Expanded view , depending on how much health and fitness information you want to see at once. In both views, you can swipe right or left to see more widgets.
Tap the + (plus) icon next to any widget you want to add to the Today page, and the - (minus) icon next to any widget you want to remove. Hiding widgets doesn't do anything to your fitness data, it just means that data isn't shown on the Today view.
You don't have to rely on your fitness tracker, smartwatch, or phone to capture all of your movement. To add something manually, tap Log on the Today view, then Activity , and pick the activity type—like Walk , Basketball , Indoor climbing , or whatever it is.
The app asks you to fill out key details, like the start and end points of the activity, before saving the record. You can manually add lots of other information from the same screens, from the hours you’ve slept to the meals you've had.
There are various parts of the Google Health interface, including the widgets on the Today page, where you'll see references to your health and fitness goals. These aren't going to be all that useful to you if you just leave the default values in place.
To make these metrics more meaningful, tap your profile picture (top right), then choose Google Health settings > Activity . You'll find numerous goals listed here, together with a few other settings, like whether or not to detect activities automatically.
Tap on any goal to set it or edit it. These targets affect the layout of screens throughout the app, and you might get notifications about them too, from time to time—if you don't want this, choose Manage notifications from the Activity screen.
You'll of course want your fitness tracker or smartwatch to be logging everything as accurately as possible. Even if the step counts are only off by a little each day, that can add up to a big difference over the weeks and months.
There are two settings to check here: If you tap your profile picture (top right), then choose Google Health settings > Activity , you can set your Stride length . This lets you give Google Health more precise measurements for your gait, whether walking or running.
Second, tap the Connections icon (top left), then your wearable. Choose Device preferences, and you can tell the app which wrist your wearable is usually on, which should mean more accurate step and movement tracking.
You may have seen mentions of Google Health Premium in the app or seen pop-ups about it, but what exactly is it? And what do you get for your money? The subscription replaces the old Fitbit Premium and works along similar lines.
For $10 a month, you get personalized and adaptable health plans that give you specific instructions for reaching your health and fitness goals. You also get a Gemini-powered AI Coach that gives you workout recaps and fitness advice based on the metrics you're recording.
The sleep summaries are more detailed in terms of sleep stages and the sleep scoring system. You also get access to a library of guided workouts and mindfulness sessions in the app.
One extra note: If you're signed up for one of Google's AI plans at the $20-per-month tier or higher, you get Google Health Premium thrown in as part of it (as well as Google Home Premium and YouTube Premium Lite).
It's possible that you want all the Google Health Premium extras but find the AI Coach a bit intrusive. It does take a very proactive stance when it comes to giving you tips and pointers, but it can be a bit too eager to help.
To hide it from view, tap your profile picture (top right), then Google Health settings > Coach . From here you can opt out of the Coach feature entirely or just hide the main insights from view. (You'll still be able to ask questions about your data.) When you need the coach’s encouragement and you want to turn it back on, you can do so in the same place.

Meta claims its Muse assistant will make users’ lives easier, but business owners say AI is driving them to go analogue
R estaurant owners are battling a horde of AI bots and returning to using the telephone instead of online booking as new virtual assistants launch in the UK – but sometimes even that isn’t enough to stop them.
This week, Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta launched its Muse AI assistant in the UK and is encouraging users to let it shop and make restaurant reservations. The bot is given access to the user’s email if they give it permission, and it can make restaurant bookings and go shopping on the user’s behalf.
Muse has been downloaded millions of times in the US, but it has caused chaos for restaurants. The online booking platform Resy has banned bots after restaurants on the platform were swarmed with agents that can refresh the page thousands of times and snap up all the reservations. Now, AI agents are plaguing venues in the UK.
Dave Strauss, the co-owner of Bouchon Racine, which was recently crowned UK restaurant of the year , said he had already had an argument with a would-be diner’s AI bot.
He answers the phones in his French restaurant every day from 11am to take reservation requests and said recently he received an unnerving call: “The other day I answered the phone to an AI bot that sounded very realistic. There was something a bit wrong about it – it sounded exactly like a human being, but something was off. I asked if it was a bot and it said: ‘Yes this is an AI booking process.’”
Strauss added: “I had an argument with the AI bot and told it to never call me again. But that wasn’t very satisfying as it didn’t argue back.”
Kimberley Coke, a high-end restaurant concierge, is paid by celebrities to secure a good table at top dining spots. She said she was worried about the swarm of AI bots: “I think it is terrifying and it could cause absolute chaos.”
Coke, who makes all her bookings via WhatsApp or phone calls, added: “There is now so much information you can get online about the hottest restaurants and where to go, and it is really hard to get the tables and that is why people come to me as I have personal relationships with the restaurants. With the apps, you don’t know who the client is, you have no background on who is coming in, they still might not show up. There is nothing worse for a restaurant in December when they have empty tables.”
Meta has claimed that its product can make people’s lives easier, but that has not been the case for the restaurants on the receiving end of the calls, emails and reservation app bookings.
The problem has been pronounced in New York City, where hard-to-secure restaurant tables are a status symbol. One of the most popular is 4 Charles Prime Rib, which serves a famous double wagyu cheeseburger, often served topped with a fried egg. It has been a popular target for AI agents, with sources at Resy saying they were having to ban multiple accounts using bots to book reservations there.
Strauss said: “There has been a constant shift to make everything as automated as possible to save a bit of money. We believe here that doesn’t work. We get a lot of emails now saying we can outsource our bookings and phone calls to AI. That makes us more keen on doing it the way that we do it. If I could get rid of online booking, I would.”
Jeremy King, who owns Simpson’s in the Strand , Arlington and the Park, said that the move towards depersonalising interactions by using AI was making him go “more analogue” in his restaurants – diners will find it much easier to snag a prime table at one of his venues by picking up the phone.
He said: “I am very happy to embrace new technology but ultimately if it conspires against us we will have to return to managing without.”
Such agents are likely to become more common in the UK and Meta has deals with an array of British businesses – including Marks & Spencer, Currys, Sainsbury’s and easyJet – allowing Muse to navigate their websites more easily and to access their apps. If a company does not offer a “connector” app that Muse can visit, the agent will access its website instead.
The Information Commissioner’s Office and the Competition and Markets Authority said they had been in talks with Meta before Muse’s launch about its responsibility to comply with UK laws. The ICO, the UK’s data protection watchdog, said on Tuesday the tech company had committed to a “voluntary monitoring and reporting scheme”, while the CMA said talks had resulted in changes to make the app’s terms and conditions fairer

Dark matter accounts for approximately 85 percent of all matter in the universe, though that’s about all we really know about the mysterious substance. Scientists believe it because of the gravitational effects it has on galaxies and other cosmic structures , but since it doesn’t otherwise interact with ordinary matter, it’s been a challenge for scientists to determine what it’s really made of.
For decades, scientists have been trying to determine whether dark matter consists of a single type of particle or if it’s made up of several particles that could have different properties and thus different interactions with the surrounding world. Earlier this year, scientists found the most convincing evidence of a dark matter particle yet, and if the second scenario is true, it’s possible we could find more.
This second possibility also raises an intriguing question: If there are a variety of “dark particles,” could they interact and combine with one another—just as the particles we know do —to form their own dark atoms and molecules? If that were the case, the dark universe could be much more complex than researchers had initially imagined.
But luckily, humanity has already faced a similar challenge in trying to understand the diversity of ordinary matter. Though to many introductory chemistry students, the periodic table can seem like an odd way to organize information, it’s one of the most ingenious tools developed in our understanding of the physical world. This classification system doesn’t just order the elements, but reveals patterns among their properties that even helped predict the existence of other elements that had not yet been discovered.
Now, a team of five physicists is exploring a scenario in which dark matter could form different classes of nuclei and atoms, governed by their own rules . Their research suggests that we may need something similar to a periodic table to understand the organization of dark matter.
The hypothesis at the heart of this research seems straight out of science fiction . The researchers propose that our universe would contain a kind of “ mirror sector ,” where particles that barely interact with visible matter have their own forces and can interact with one another.
The idea is not new and is quite serious. The “Mirror Twin Higgs” was proposed two decades ago as a possible solution to a problem related to the mass of the Higgs boson . According to this theory, mirror particles would help offset certain quantum effects that might otherwise cause its mass to be much greater than what we observe . Although the existence of these particles has never been proven, the proposal offered an ingenious way to address the problem without requiring all new particles to be visible to detectors .
One of the creators of the Mirror Twin Higgs theory, physicist Zackaria Chacko, is part of this new investigation that extends this hypothesis into the dark matter puzzle. Along with several collaborators, he explores in this recent preprint what would happen if particles from this hypothetical mirror sector could combine with one another, forming nuclei, atoms, and a variety of dark elements.
Their calculations suggest that, under certain conditions, these particles could combine to form dark equivalents of some of the elements we know, ranging from the simplest to others as complex as carbon. However, this would not be an exact copy of our matter . The dark particles would have different masses and properties, which would also change the rules governing how they bond, what structures they can form , and which ones remain stable.
For example, in the researchers’ model, dark hydrogen atoms would be unstable and could not survive as those in our universe do. This is a striking difference when we consider that hydrogen is the simplest and most abundant element in ordinary matter.
If these dark elements were ever discovered, understanding the rules governing their formation would be essential for classifying them. A sort of “dark periodic table” could help bring order to that diversity, just as it did with the elements we know.
For now, this all remains in the realm of theoretical physics . Researchers have not observed any of these atoms, and some doubt such structures could actually form. But there’s plenty about dark matter we have yet to discover.
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

Tech billionaires are taking us for a ride. But new ‘poison pill’ software could help shield human-made creative output from hijacking
Grand Theft Auto VI came out on the same day that Anthropic made its stock market debut. I keep thinking about that coincidence. As more than one tech writer has pointed out, the new GTA took 13 years to make, more than $1bn of investment and involved 9,000 sets of human hands, and it will probably be the last blockbuster video game to be fully free of generative AI.
On the day of its release, a group chat with my most gaming-minded male friends erupted in discussion about whether or not video games, and GTA VI specifically, rose to the level of art. Exploring a national park? Yes, that’s there . Badly assemble a coffee table from “Krapea” (the game’s fictional furniture company)? Ditto. Eating a hot dog? Why not. All of it gloriously human in origin. Perhaps that in itself is an argument for how GTA VI crosses the blurry line from entertainment to something more. It is a medium by which human beings offer others a (necessarily incomplete) interpretation of what it’s like to be them in the world, or to try to transcend it.
At the very least, Grand Theft Auto is a franchise that has always offered at least a glimmer of social critique – even in its early 2000s iterations – amid its otherwise overwhelming scope for virtual hedonism and violence. Olivier Mauco, a French political scientist and author of GTA IV: the Flipside of the American Dream, sees that 2008 version of the game as a turning point : away from pure provocation and towards an acerbic dissection of US aspiration, which remains out of reach for the game’s immigrant protagonist, who has fled war in the Balkans and remains forever marginalised.
In this latest version, Jason and Lucia experience the same “ desperation capitalism ” that might induce you to try to trade your way out of a broken, oligarchic economy – or just want to burn the system down. At the same time, there is no shortage of laments from far-right gamer bros who find the storyline and gameplay too “woke”, because it nudges players towards an empathetic and balanced romantic partnership, rather than a misogynistic one – even while also allowing you to run over elderly people with their own mobility scooters just for the hell of it.
As Wired points out , GTA VI “is bristling with parodies of toxic manosphere content and crypto scams. Random characters on the street will spout Maga-coded conspiracy theories and call you a ‘libtard’ or ‘commie socialist’ if you walk into them … Yet the provocation of asking guys to consider acts of service for a virtual girlfriend could prove the most revolutionary element.”
Whether Rockstar Games , the company behind the GTA franchise, timed it on purpose or not, it feels pertinent that on the same day that tens of millions were entering an all-encompassing virtual space where cars, bicycles, airplanes and boats are there for the taking, the most lucrative grand cultural theft in human history was playing out in the markets. Generative AI would be impossible without having vacuumed up almost the sum total of human creative output. All of our words, music, paintings; our attempts to deal with the emotional experience of the world, have been “acquired” and handed to an algorithm incapable of either emotion or experience.
Journalism is one victim of AI “scraping” cannibalising the providers of expensive-to-produce reporting. Here in France, where Google’s AI Overview was legally blocked until July, the impact on newspapers has been devastating and swift : for Libération, a decline in site visits of more than 30%, and nearly 20% for Le Monde.
Stories abound from writers whose books were pirated by Anthropic and others, and to whom Anthropic offered an insultingly low settlement : a mere 0.1% of the company’s valuation at its IPO, or roughly $3,000 (£2,300) per pirated work (of which publishers will then take half). Even to acquire that paltry $1,500, many writers have spent months jumping through bureaucratic hoops trying to get paid. Meanwhile, Anthropic’s seven co-founders have hauled in paper fortunes worth $180bn, and even an average employee could now be worth more than $40m.
In the real world, the world of Grand Theft Anthropic , nobody is coming to save us. The courts have too often abdicated the spirit of the law meant to protect creative works. Governments have ceded common sense to an oligarchic billionaire class, and the avaricious logic that always demands more, when it comes to data centres and compute.
Last week, I had a video call with Gabriel and Isaque, the Brazilian co-developers of a piece of software called ShieldFont , an open-source project hoping to protect content written by humans by “poisoning” unauthorised AI training. ShieldFont uses a dictionary of nearly 12,000 words that it scrambles when they are detected in writing, in such a way that the result seems grammatically and semantically legible, all while actually being nonsense. When the text is rendered visually, we read the correct version, while an AI scraping webpage ingests the “poisoned” text, which corrupts its dataset.
The pair originally created ShieldFont to protect their own website, but then realised that by making it open-source (meaning, for example, that media organisations could keep their own custom typefaces and still implement ShieldFont), it could potentially become a meaningful deterrent against non-consensual scraping. “I was thinking of the song Toxicity by System of a Down, and the line that goes ‘How do you own disorder?’,” Gabriel told me. “Of course, you can’t own disorder, and so the idea was to use chaos as a tool against chaos.”
The pair stressed to me that their intent is to fight unauthorised AI scraping, not AI as a whole. But considering how much unauthorised and unethical scraping already underlies the trillion-dollar AI industry, I can’t help but have a more mischievous, more GTA-worthy thought. Taken as a whole, news organisations (including this one) and Wikipedia are sitting on billions of lines of text. If these sites were wholesale converted to ShieldFont and then scraped, it would be a first shot fired at poisoning the data well of generative AI.
Like in Grand Theft Auto, these companies and their billionaires have hijacked the car and they’re taking us for a ride. In life, as in the game, chaos abounds. But in Grand Theft Anthropic, we are not NPCs: non-player characters. So maybe it’s time to grab the wheel.
