Kindles are getting costlier faster than they’re getting better.
Supply pressures, shortages, and inflation have pushed tech prices relentlessly upward over the last half-decade, and even basic gadgets haven’t been immune. That’s why you can spend $385 on a Raspberry Pi, or why the cheapest Amazon Kindle in 2026 costs more than the midrange one from a few years ago . “New thing, better features, same price” used to be a reliable formula, but now you’re lucky if you can get the same thing for barely more than before.
The 2024 Kindles all came with small price increases, but the 2026 models make them look like stellar deals. The $160 Kindle Paperwhite from two years ago wipes the floor with this year’s $150 Kindle in just about every conceivable way, from screen size to front light quality to waterproofing—something to consider if you’re choosing between a used or refurbished Paperwhite and one of these new models.
The flagship of the now five-model-large monochrome Kindle family is the $250 2026 Paperwhite Signature Edition, which takes the core specs of the new $200 Paperwhite and puts it in a sturdy iPad-esque aluminum case instead of the typical plastic.
It’s an exceptionally nice reader, and if you’re down with paying even more for it, longtime page-turn button holdouts can recover their precious buttons while still getting the benefits of new, fast Kindle hardware. With the exception of one regression—wireless charging, a feature of the 2024 Signature Edition that has been removed here—it’s the fastest and nicest Kindle you can get. It’s mostly the value, or lack thereof, that leaves a bad taste in one’s mouth.
Unlike the 2021 or 2024 Kindle Paperwhite updates, the 2026 Paperwhite doesn’t include any notable screen or lighting upgrades. Anyone upgrading from a two- or three-generation-old version of the hardware will still get an upgrade, but the 2026 Paperwhite isn’t doing a ton to push the category forward. And while speed increases were front-and-center in Amazon’s promotional material for the 2024 Paperwhite, Amazon isn’t highlighting any particular gains for this year’s Paperwhite (the base Kindle does apparently open books 30 percent faster than the previous-generation Kindle, though).
But the Paperwhite and this year’s basic Kindle both make a couple of tweaks worth mentioning that don’t really show up on a spec sheet. One is that the device’s power button moves from the bottom edge to the top-right edge, a small change I appreciate because I’ve accidentally pressed the bottom-mounted power button all the times I’ve tried to set the Kindle on the edge of something. The other is that the devices now have user-replaceable batteries, a change made in part to comply with right-to-repair regulations going into effect in some countries.
Whether you’re buying the standard plastic-backed Paperwhite or the aluminum Signature Edition, you’re still getting a 7-inch 300 PPI screen with a front light that can adjust its color temperature as well as its brightness, which I find makes the Paperwhite easier on the eyes than the harsher, more bluish-tinted front light on older Kindles and the basic 2026 Kindle. The plastic Paperwhite is a smidge lighter than the 2024 version, and the Signature Edition is a little heavier (thanks in part to the aluminum casing), though not by a lot in either direction.
Whether it’s faster than the 2024 Paperwhite or not, the snappy and fluid performance I observed while using that device is definitely present in this one. The E-Ink screen still puts a cap on exactly how fluid and responsive the device can feel, but you rarely feel the big gap between your touch input and the device responding to that input like you can on most older Kindles. (I tried repeatedly to run the old Google Octane 2.0 benchmark I used to get a sense of the 2024 Paperwhite’s relative performance, but it could never complete a run in either the 2026 Kindle or the 2026 Paperwhite’s browser, for whatever reason).
I didn’t spend as much time with it, but I did test the basic 6-inch Kindle alongside the Paperwhite Signature Edition.
Overall, I like the updated look and feel of the redesigned Kindle, particularly the fact that the screen and bezel are now flush, as the last few Paperwhites have been. And despite using the same 6-inch screen size as older Paperwhites, Amazon has significantly shrunk the overall size and weight of the device. It doesn’t quite look like a “Kindle mini” next to the current Paperwhite, but it’s not far off.
But you’re still getting less for your money than you were a few years ago. If you compare the 2026 Kindle to the 2024 or 2022 model, and you ignore what each one of those devices cost to buy, it looks like slow and steady improvement. But the fact is that you can pay $150 for this Kindle and lose important features, like the warm light and waterproofing, that Amazon offered in the 2021 Paperwhite for just $140 back in 2021.
That’s just the reality of buying technology right now. “Get more for the same money” is out. Now if you want more, you have to pay more.
The new Paperwhite Signature Edition’s biggest upgrade, should you choose to pay for it, is the addition of page-turn buttons. Page-turn buttons by proxy, at least.
The Signature Edition adds iPad-style copper contacts on the back, and for another $80 (on top of the $250 you’ll pay for the Kindle) you can buy a Kindle Page Turn Cover in various colors that connects to those contacts with pogo pins. It’s the cover that adds the buttons. Amazon also offers a $60 charging stand that uses the pins, the closest equivalent for the now-removed wireless charging feature.
The cover really does make the new Paperwhite look and feel a bit more like a Frankenstein Kindle Oasis, right down to the asymmetrical edge that the button area adds. And the page-turn buttons themselves feel good and work well. The physical feedback from clicky buttons and the Kindle’s overall responsiveness both make page turns feel nearly instantaneous when you press it to turn a single page. Clicking the buttons quickly to turn multiple pages still gets bogged down a little.
Functionally, the worst things I can say about the Page Turn Cover are that it adds to the reader’s size and weight, and the power button doesn’t feel nearly as good as the page-turn buttons. The case’s “button” is basically a little plastic nub that pushes in the device’s actual built-in power button. At least with the hardware I bought, the case’s button feels like it can’t consistently reach the device button, which means it wasn’t always reliable. This is partly moot because opening and closing the cover also wakes and sleeps the device.
Amazon offers one cheaper option for every other Kindle that can run the newest version of the Kindle operating system: a $35 remote control-style Kindle Click . As a completely separate accessory you have to hold or rest on something in order to use, I don’t find this to be a particularly compelling solution to the “no buttons” problem. But it’s also the only version of “clickable buttons” that Amazon offers for less than $330. It is what it is.
The Kindle Click requires a Kindle running version 5.20.1.0.2 or later of the Kindle operating system. Currently, that version only runs on the 2024 and 2026 Kindles, plus 2022’s Kindle Scribe. It seems as though Amazon has gotten stingier with long-tail Kindle OS updates than it was in 2024, when all Kindles going back to 2018 could run the same software. The 2018 Kindles currently top out at 5.18, while the other 2021/22 Kindles stop at 5.19.
The last reader Amazon offered with page-turn buttons was 2019’s $249 Kindle Oasis, which was dinged pretty much across the board for being “expensive.” Today’s Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition will cost you just as much, but charge you $80 extra for the case and buttons. It’s a nicer reader in some important ways, most notably its USB-C port and much-improved performance. But that’s still a pretty substantia…

The Motley Fool is the O.G. stock and investment advice website, dating back to the early days of the Internet, when WIRED’s website was still called hotwired.com . It started as a tip sheet in the early ‘90s by brothers Tom and David Gardner, and it rode a wave of hype to become a cult phenomenon, viewed with equal interest and skepticism by the established investment class. Subscriptions to the basic Stock Advisor tips are quite reasonable on a weekly basis, but more sophisticated analysis is also available for professionals and high-volume investors at premium prices. Médecins Sans Frontières says the number of its staff who have been killed in Gaza has risen to 17
Two workers for the medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) have been killed in an Israeli strike in Gaza, according to the organisation.
MSF said the strike was a direct hit on one of the charity's clinics, the location of which was known by the Israeli military.
In a statement, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said the two people were Hamas operatives "acting as security guards at a clinic operated by MSF". The IDF added the strike was "not directed at a hospital" and caused no damage to medical infrastructure.
The head of the World Health Organization (WHO) said that attacks on health facilities and health workers in Gaza were "outrageous and unacceptable".
In a post on X, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus wrote: "Those risking their lives to save others must be protected, not attacked."
In its statement, MSF - which is also known as Doctors Without Borders - said that the two workers who were killed were watchmen, and added that the strike brought the number of its colleagues killed in Gaza to 17.
The organisation said it was "devastated and outraged" and added: "​Our premises were clearly marked with MSF logos, and their location had been communicated to and was known by the Israeli military."
In its own post on X, the IDF said that the two men, who they named as Ahmed Sufyan Muhammad Ali Abu Hasira and Moaz Yousef Alitsbach, were "terrorists in Hamas' military wing".
The Israeli military added it was another example of Hamas "embedding itself within international organizations".
It said that "precautionary measures were taken to minimize harm to civilians" before the strike on Gaza City, adding the men had "advanced plans to carry out attacks against Israeli civilians & IDF troops".
Witnesses told the BBC the two men were sitting at the clinic entrance when an Israeli drone descended and fired a missile.
Video footage from the scene of the strike showed a small crater beside a plastic chair, with bloodstains and limited damage in a courtyard behind the medical clinic.
Hundreds of Palestinians have since attended the funeral of the MSF workers, carrying the two bodies, wrapped in white plastic bags and placed on stretchers, on their shoulders as they made their way through the streets of the city.
Mohammed Imad, a close friend of Abu Hasira, one of the men killed, said he had seen him just hours before the attack.
"He was a peaceful, kind-hearted man. His only concern was looking after his wife, his two children and his mother," he told the BBC.
He said Abu Hasira had no affiliation with any armed group and had worked at the clinic for a long time.
The two workers' deaths follow an increase in Israeli strikes across Gaza over the past week.
Gaza's civil defence spokesman said eight Palestinians were killed in Israeli attacks across the Strip during the day, including the two MSF workers.
Violence has continued in Gaza since Israel and Hamas agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire in October last year. Israeli strikes take place almost daily in areas under the control of Hamas, which are home to 2.1 million people, most of them displaced.
At least 1,705 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The humanitarian situation also remains dire, with heavy rainfall earlier this month causing flooding and damage to tens of thousands of shelters for displaced families.
The UN and its partners have called on Israel - which controls Gaza's crossings - to allow in more supplies to help Palestinians prepare for the winter, including tents, heaters and water pumps, as well as vaccines and medicines to combat infectious diseases.
The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,770 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

Voters across Taiwan have cast ballots for mayors, council members and other local leaders.
The candidate for Taiwan’s opposition Kuomintang party (KMT) has secured re-election in the mayoral race for the capital, Taipei, after his main rival conceded defeat.
Voters on Saturday cast ballots for some 11,000 positions across Taiwan’s 16 counties and “six municipalities”, or largest cities, in local elections closely watched by China, which considers the self-ruling island to be a part of its territory and has pledged reunification by force if necessary.
The DPP looked set to clinch half of the municipalities, taking back Taichung – the island’s second most populous city – along with Tainan and Kaohsiung.
But its Taipei candidate, academic Puma Shen, conceded defeat late on Saturday to incumbent Chiang Wan-an of the KMT. Chiang won by a double-digit margin in the previous election and is seen as a possible future presidential candidate.
In addition to the capital, the KMT is likely to win the other two municipalities: New Taipei City, the most populous of the six municipalities, and Taoyuan.
Election campaigns ahead of the vote centred on domestic issues including transport, childcare and the environment, rather than disputed ties with China.
The KMT traditionally favours closer ties with Beijing, while the ruling DPP rejects China’s sovereignty claims. KMT chairwoman Cheng Li-wun met Chinese President Xi Jinping in April.
Taiwan’s Ministry of National Defence said 33 Chinese warplanes encircled Taiwan on Friday, including bombers and fighter jets, along with eight warships.
The KMT dominated the last local elections, winning across 14 cities and counties. The DPP managed only 5, while other parties and independents took 3.
Preparations and campaigns for the 2028 presidential and parliamentary elections are expected to start after Saturday’s election results.
President William Lai Ching-te of the DPP is likely to run again, while outgoing Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen could be the KMT’s frontrunner.

An international tribunal refuses Buenos Aires’s application, giving green light for the project off the disputed region.
An international court has rejected Argentina’s request for provisional measures to halt United Kingdom-authorised oil drilling near the Falkland Islands.
Saturday’s ruling by the United Nations-backed International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea is a setback to Buenos Aires’s latest effort to challenge economic activity around the disputed territory.
Argentina’s request marks the latest spat between the two countries, which fought a brief but bitter 74-day war in 1982 over the UK-administered islands in the South Atlantic.
In September, Argentina launched an arbitration process against London over the Sea Lion project off the Falklands, which is led by the UK’s Rockhopper company and Israel’s Navitas.
Buenos Aires has argued the plan violates a UN resolution calling for both sides to desist from unilateral actions until their dispute over the sovereignty of the islands is resolved.
It has asked the court to impose emergency measures and order the UK to take the necessary steps “to ensure that no new drilling for exploitation, and no installation of production infrastructure” takes place in the North Malvinas Basin.
It further urged the Hamburg-based court, an independent court set up under UN auspices, to order the UK to “refrain from using the information obtained in the exploration of the natural resources of the disputed maritime areas”.
The Sea Lion oil field is located about 220km (135 miles) from the islands, which lie 600km (372 miles) off Argentina’s Patagonian coast and almost 13,000km (8,077 miles) from the UK.
Argentinian President Javier Milei has doubled down on his country’s claim over the Falklands – known in Argentina as Las Malvinas – since US President Donald Trump said he was open to reviewing Washington’s stance on the territory.
Reacting to the ruling, he said Buenos Aires will continue its efforts to halt the project.
“This decision is not the final word,” Milei said in a statement, noting that Argentina will continue to “assert its rights through all diplomatic, legal and administrative channels at its disposal.”
The Falkland Islanders themselves voted overwhelmingly in 2013 to remain part of the UK.
But Argentina rejects that outcome, arguing the principle of self-determination does not apply to a population it considers implanted by the UK after 1833.
The UK, meanwhile, has urged the court to reject the case, saying it was rooted in Argentina’s claims to sovereignty.
London argues the sovereignty claim falls outside the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea’s arbitration process aimed at settling maritime disputes.
The UK government’s chief legal adviser, Ellie Reeves, told the judges in a two-day hearing earlier this month that the order sought by Argentina “would prevent the people of the Falkland Islands from developing their natural resources, as they are entitled to do so”.
This could have “devastating” economic consequences for the islanders, she said, adding that what Argentina “wants is to take control of those resources for itself”.
Britain’s Prime Minister Andy Burnham also raised the Sea Lion project with Trump in a call in late October.
“The prime minister raised the economic consequences of Argentina’s coercive measures for the UK and US and reiterated the importance of respecting the islanders’ right to develop their natural resources,” Burnham’s office said in a statement.
The tribunal was set up under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), which came into force in 1994 and which sets out a “regime of law and order in the world’s oceans and seas, establishing rules governing all uses of the oceans and their resources”.
If the court orders provisional emergency measures, these would be legally binding on both parties.

Argentina's bid to block an oil exploration project near the Falkland Islands has been rejected by a UN-backed international tribunal.
The Argentinian government had called for the Sea Lion venture to be halted as it claimed there was an ongoing dispute over the sovereignty of the Falklands, a British overseas territory. The UK has repeatedly rejected that claim.
Speaking on Saturday, the president of the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea said it was the wrong court to rule on questions of sovereignty. The decision was upheld in a vote 18-3.
After the ruling, Argentina's President Javier Milei said "this decision is not the final word" and declared "the Falkland Islands are Argentine".
In a joint statement, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and Attorney General Ellie Reeves said that Buenos Aires must "respect the right of the Falkland Islanders to determine their own future".
"Argentina sought to stop the Falkland Islanders making their own sovereign decisions and failed in this attempt," they wrote, urging Argentina to "end its wider economic pressure" against the territory.
The case is the latest diplomatic row between the UK and Argentina, which fought a 74-day war over the islands in 1982.
The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles (209 km) from the Falkland Islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil.
Two oil companies – Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum – are due to begin extracting from the oilfield within two years, potentially generating huge revenues for the roughly 3,500 inhabitants of the islands.
But the Argentinian government claimed the marine environment of disputed maritime areas is protected by international law, arguing that while it believed there was a territorial dispute over the Falklands, nothing should be done that could change the situation - including the building of oil wells.
The UK responded that the Law of the Sea court had no jurisdiction over the issue, and that pausing the Sea Lion project could have huge economic consequences on the islands' local population and companies connected with the venture.
The tribunal's decision ultimately rested on its own powers - this was a territorial issue, and a maritime court was not the right place to hear the dispute.
Buenos Aires disagreed, writing in a statement after the decision that "Argentina did not ask the court to rule on sovereignty", but to apply the United Nations' sea laws to the UK over its "exploitation of our resources".
It also said that five individuals would face sanctions for their involvement in the oil drilling venture, something Milei had been threatening . The statement did not specify who the sanctions would be against.
"The message is clear: those who participate in the illegal exploitation of our resources will face the consequences," the statement said.
The 10-week war that was fought in 1982 started when Argentine forces landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim over the islands, as a British military task force fought to eject them.
The conflict led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine military personnel.
Despite its defeat, Argentina has always maintained its right to the Falklands, and over the years, successive governments have pressed their claim with varying degrees of aggression and diplomacy.
The UK government has made clear that sovereignty remains with Britain and maintains that the island's population has a right to self-determination.
In a 2013 referendum, residents of the islands voted overwhelmingly to remain a British overseas territory - with 99.8% voting in favour and just three voting against.

UK government calls on Buenos Aires to end ‘economic pressure’ on islands after international tribunal’s ruling
The UK has called on Argentina to stop its economic warfare on the Falkland islands after Buenos Aires failed in a legal attempt to terminate an offshore oil project vital to the future of the British overseas territory.
An application by the South American country for suspension of the Sea Lion project was rejected on Saturday by the international tribunal for the law of the seas (Itlos) on the grounds that the issue lay outside its jurisdiction.
In a joint statement, Ed Miliband , the UK’s foreign secretary and Ellie Reeves, the attorney general for England and Wales, said: “Argentina sought to stop the Falkland Islanders making their own sovereign decisions and failed in this attempt.
“The UK has no doubt of our sovereignty of the Falkland Islands , our sovereignty and sovereign rights over the surrounding maritime areas, and the right of self-determination of the Falkland Islanders.
“We now call on Argentina to respect the right of the Falkland Islanders to determine their own future and urge Argentina to end its wider economic pressure against the Falkland Islands.”
The ruling from Itlos is a significant blow to Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, who has described reclaiming sovereignty of the Falkland islands, known in Argentina as Las Malvinas, as a “national cause”.
The Falklands has a prosperous economy but the Sea Lion oil project is said to offer the potential to double the islands’ GDP. It is seen by the Falkland Islands’ government as a vital way to secure its future as a self-financed British overseas territory.
Milei has previously said that blocking the drilling is part of a wider strategy to force the UK into talks over sovereignty over the archipelago, over which the two countries went to war in 1982 after an invasion by Argentinian forces.
In a decision read out on Saturday by the president of Itlos, Maurice Kamga, the tribunal rejected Argentina’s arguments for a suspension of the project, saying there did not appear to be any basis for believing it had jurisdiction as the tribunal was unable to rule on questions of sovereignty.
Kamga said 18 judges had voted to reject Argentina’s claims, while three had voted to uphold them. At a hearing earlier this month, Argentina said drilling should not be allowed until the issue of sovereignty over the islands had been resolved and asked Itlos to issue a temporary injunction until a full arbitration hearing could be held.
Mario Oyarzábal, the chief legal adviser to Argentina’s ministry of foreign affairs, had claimed that the oil money from the drilling would “finance the very military base and presence that sustains the UK’s de facto control of the territory”.
During the two-day hearing, Reeves said that such an order would have “devastating consequences” for the islanders and prevent them from developing their natural resources “as they are entitled to do so, pursuant to their fundamental right to self-determination”.
The Sea Lion project in the North Falkland basin, led by the Israeli company Navitas and its British partner, Rockhopper, will start drilling in March, and oil will be extracted from 2028 and continue for 35 years. It has the potential to double the islands’ GDP, with a cumulative uplift of £8bn over the lifetime of the project.
Milei previously described the companies’ activities as unlawful and launched economic sanctions on people and firms involved in oil exploration around the islands.
An arbitration tribunal will now address the substance of the dispute, but its decision could take years, and by then oil exploitation will have already begun. The Argentinian government is pushing through legislation that would criminalise parties involved in the Falklands economy.
In a statement, a spokesperson for Milei claimed that the tribunal’s ruling was not the “final word” on the dispute, adding: “By history and by right: the Malvinas are Argentine.”
The spokesperson said: “The decision by the international tribunal for the law of the sea in no way legitimises the unilateral exploitation of our natural resources. The national government will continue to take all necessary actions to prevent such exploitation. In this regard, new sanction proceedings were initiated yesterday against five entities for violations of our current legal framework. The message is clear: those who participate in the illegitimate exploitation of our resources must face the consequences.
“The defence of our sovereignty is not the cause of any single government or political party; it is an inalienable constitutional mandate. Argentina will continue to assert its rights through all available diplomatic, legal, and administrative channels, with the firm conviction that no unilateral action by the United Kingdom can extinguish our legitimate sovereign rights.”
A spokesperson for Navitas said: “We welcome the tribunal’s decision to reject all of Argentina’s requests for provisional measures. Navitas remains focused on the continued responsible development of the Sea Lion project, pursuant to licences issued by the Falkland Islands government. We wish to extend our appreciation for the UK government’s continued and unwavering support for the Falkland Islands and the Sea Lion project.”

After media reports of a breach into the US Air Force's flagship cloud computing platform, the US military issued a statement on Friday denying any issues with its computer security.
"The Department of War's systems are safe, secure, and managed 24-7 by the best experts and teams in the world. We will continue to maintain all mission-critical operations and applications," a Defence Department official said.
"As a matter of policy and operations security, the Department of War does not comment on the status of our networks," a Defence Department official said earlier on Friday.
Although the Pentagon did not specifically answer whether the Air Force's Cloud One platform had been hacked, sources told Reuters the Cloud One platform breach was discovered the past month.
This breach, which could jeopardise a swathe of sensitive tactical, personal and logistical data, led to disruption across the platform, according to these sources, quoted by Reuters.
The US Air Force's Cloud-Based Command and Control platform is used for air defence radar, data feeds from across North America and combat systems, which track bombs and missiles across more than 200 US Air Force locations around the world, according to Reuters.
NBC News reported on Friday that the cloud platform was hacked and that the attack "could have exposed sensitive military information." Federal News Network, a media covering US federal agencies, also reported the breach through a source "familiar with the incident."
Cloud One has been the target of hackers for a long time. In 2023, the platform's leadership boasted a "100% success rate" in beating attempts to breach the platform.
In recent weeks, the CIA and FBI were also reportedly subject to hacks along with suppliers for major American financial institutions including JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Mastercard.
Microsoft Outlook, US air traffic control and a top-secret NSA network also suffered issues recently, with officials at pains to blame the outages on maintenance or defects — not intrusions.
But these tech outages are not limited to the US; the European Commission was cyberattacked in October by an AI-assisted hack.

Socialist PM Pedro Sánchez’s high-stakes gamble could end in defeat to a coalition including the far-right Vox
Spaniards head to the polls on Sunday to vote in a high-stakes snap general election that could put a far-right party in government for the first time since the country’s return to democracy after the death of Gen Francisco Franco in 1975.
Although the next election was not due until summer next year, Spain’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, called the vote in October after three rightwing and far-right parties voted down the emergency legislation that his government had proposed to address the country’s housing crisis .
Huge public anger over soaring rents exploded in September after the eviction of María del Carmen Abascal , an 87-year-old woman who was removed from her home in Madrid because she could not afford the 230% rent increase demanded by the investment fund that had bought her apartment.
Faced with nationwide protests, Sánchez’s coalition minority government put together a package of measures aimed at improving access to housing, from a ban on evictions until 2030 to the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room.
Sánchez opted for one of his characteristic gambles and announced the early election after the proposals were torpedoed by the conservative People’s party (PP), the far-right Vox and the rightwing Catalan separatist Junts.
The prime minister – an inveterate risk-taker whose penchant for unpredictable moves has fuelled his political survival – calculated that his opponents’ decision to block the housing overhauls could work in his electoral favour.
On Friday morning, Sánchez said he was confident of victory. “I can’t conceive of us losing,” he told Cadena Ser radio , adding: “When progressive Spain gets going, it’s unstoppable.”
But while his Spanish Socialist Workers’ party (PSOE) has managed to narrow the distance between it and the PP, which is leading the polls, to fewer than three percentage points, the right looks likely to form the next government in coalition with the far right.
Survey after survey predicts the PP will finish first but fall short of a majority, leaving it dependent on a deal with Vox. Between them, the two parties are forecast to secure a joint majority well above the 176 required seats in Spain’s 350-seat congress of deputies. Even if the PSOE enjoys a last-minute surge and comes first, the parliamentary arithmetic suggests it would struggle to cobble together another coalition administration with the support of its allies in the leftwing Broad Front alliance and with that of regional nationalist parties.
Choosing housing as a key battleground allowed Sánchez to attempt to shift the focus away from the corruption allegations facing his inner circle. It also offered him the chance to move on from his government’s much-criticised handling of the crisis in Spain’s north African territory of Ceuta , which was sparked when about 80,000 people crossed into the territory from neighbouring Morocco in the space of 48 hours.
But some of the energy of the government’s resurgent campaign was sapped at the end of October when 69 people were killed in Spain’s second deadly rail crash in just nine months .
The PP and Vox have used the two crashes to accuse the government of failing in its basic duty to keep Spaniards safe. More broadly, the PP and Vox are using the poll as a referendum on what they disdainfully refer to as “ sanchismo ”. They argue that the style of government favoured by the prime minister and his allies is cynical, corrupt, opportunistic and self-serving.
“Spain deserves a decent prime minister and [Sánchez] isn’t one,” the PP leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, told viewers during a head-to-head debate between the two men last week.
Sánchez, however, insisted that while he had made errors, Spain was in a better state than it was when he came to office in 2018. “My government hasn’t been perfect; I’ve made mistakes,” he said. “But I’m also fully aware that we have always governed in the right direction.”
The prime minister has also sought to depict the snap election as a stark choice between progressive forces and reactionary ones – as typified by the PP’s putative alliance with Vox.
“You must decide whether you want our country to move backwards or continue moving forwards, and whether you prefer a government that works for the interests of the majority of society,” he told Spaniards as he announced the vote.
Over recent days, the government has tried to underline its commitment to social justice and equality by proposing a new tax on fortunes of more than €100m (£84m) that would help fund childcare, housing and public services.
The PP, meanwhile, is promising to lower taxes, build 1m homes, and “restore the country’s ambition and self-esteem”. Vox’s manifesto , which includes plans to have Sánchez and his government prosecuted “for treason and crimes against the security of the state” over the Ceuta mass crossing, focuses on deregulation, “remigration” and giving Spanish-born people priority over those born abroad for housing and public services.
Although the PP’s previous leader, Pablo Casado, famously repudiated Vox and its ideology, accusing the party of practising a politics based on “fear, anger, resentment and revenge” , the PP has repeatedly entered into regional coalition governments with Vox and now runs four of Spain’s autonomous regions with the party.
In recent days, the PP and Vox have attempted to call into question the fairness and transparency of the election, making baseless claims that the government may seek to rig postal votes. Vox’s leader, Santiago Abascal, has also suggested, without providing evidence, that Sánchez is working to undermine democracy and change the country’s demographic makeup .

Francesca Albanese, leading critic of Israeli abuses in Gaza and West Bank, barred on ‘national security grounds’
Costa Rica barred entry to the UN special rapporteur on the Israel-occupied Palestinian territories, Francesca Albanese, earning the ire of the UN human rights chief.
Albanese, an Italian national, went to Costa Rica to receive an honorary doctorate from the University of Costa Rica. She was stopped at the airport in San José and not allowed to enter the country, and was transferred to a hotel before she travelled to Mexico on Saturday.
The UN human rights office said that Albanese was stopped from entering the country on “national security grounds”. Costa Rica’s migration office said that its decision was made after she was subject of an “alert” over alleged ties to terrorism.
The UN high commissioner for human rights, Volker Türk, said that he was “deeply concerned” by the decision to deny Albanese entry. “This is difficult to reconcile with Costa Rica’s longstanding commitment to human rights,” said Türk.
Albanese shared a picture on X of an airport bench and her suitcase, where she was meant to stay the night. “Second night in the airport. Guarded by security at every step. Uncomfortable chairs. Noise. Bright light,” Albanese posted.
Albanese, who acts as an independent expert appointed by the UN human rights council, has been outspoken on Israeli abuses in Gaza and the West Bank . She has drawn ire from Israel and its allies for being one of the first, most prominent officials to accuse Israel of committing genocide in Gaza – a claim Israel denies.
The US placed sanctions and revoked the visa of Albanese for her work on Palestine in the summer of 2025, cutting her off from the global financial system. The sanctions make daily life a struggle for Albanese, who has no access to western banks or credit cards.
Albanese called for an investigation into whether her denial of entry into Costa Rica was connected to the US sanctions, in remarks she made remotely at the ceremony for the acceptance of her honorary doctorate.
Costa Rica’s government, headed by the rightwing president, Laura Fernández, is close to the Trump administration and has cooperated with it on security and immigration issues. The government has also intensified its ties with Israel.
Israel’s envoy to the UN, Danny Danon, praised Costa Rica for its decision, accusing Albanese of using her UN position to spread propaganda against Israel.
On Saturday, Albanese was expected leave Costa Rica for Mexico, with the Italian embassy in Mexico working in advance of her visit to ensure there are no obstacles to her entry into the country.

Socialist PM Pedro Sanchez seeks re-election but polls have suggested conservative PP and far-right Vox could reach threshold for majority.
Madrid, Spain – Voters in Spain are set to head to the polls in an election that could open the door to the far right entering the country’s national government, half a century after the end of Francisco Franco’s dictatorship.
After a bitter campaign largely focused on housing and immigration, Sunday’s snap vote pits two sharply different accounts of socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s eight years in power against each other. One says the country has become a bastion of social progress and a driver of economic growth in a largely stagnant Europe. The other, embraced by the opposition conservatives and the far right, says Spain needs a profound change after years of alleged corruption and opportunism.
“They [the elections] have been framed in plebiscitary terms, as a vote for or against Pedro Sanchez’s leadership,” Alvaro Sanchez-Garcia, a political scientist and postdoctoral fellow at Spain’s Centre for Political and Constitutional Studies, told Al Jazeera. In a campaign this polarising, he said, voters who switch parties tend to stay within the same bloc, with only a few crossing from left to right or the other way around.
Polls suggest the conservative People’s Party (PP) will win most seats but will need the far-right Vox party – projected to finish third – to secure the 176 seats required for an outright majority in the 350-seat Congress of Deputies. Most surveys suggest the PP and Vox would reach that number together, giving PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo a path to power through either a coalition or a minority government backed by Vox in parliament.
Despite the unfavourable predictions, Sanchez has expressed optimism that left-leaning voters will mobilise in large numbers come election day to prevent a right-wing surge. In 2023, his PSOE had finished second but Sanchez secured another term with support from parties to his left, and Catalan and Basque groupings.
“I can’t conceive of us losing,” he said in a radio interview on Friday, before addressing supporters at his final campaign rally in the capital, Madrid: “This election about one thing only: Whether Spain moves forward or goes backwards.”
In power since 2018, Sanchez says Spain has never been in a better shape, pointing to the dynamism of the country’s economy. The European Commission forecasts growth of 2.6 percent for Spain this year, compared with 1.2 percent for the eurozone.
Sanchez has become a popular figure among Europe’s progressives at a time of a wider shift to the right across the European Union. The 54-year-old has frequently clashed with US President Donald Trump, refused to increase defence spending to 5 percent as requested by other NATO members and called Israel’s war in Gaza a genocide.
But at home, not everyone sees him the same way. “People abroad think he is a hero, but not here,” said Isabel Labayen, a longtime PP voter. “How is it possible that we are praised abroad but people [in Spain] can’t afford a house, food or have doctor appointments in months rather than days?” the 64-year-old asked. “We have a problem.”
Housing was also what brought the election forward. Sanchez called the snap vote in October after parliament rejected two measures intended to protect renters following protests over high housing costs and evictions.
Opponents say Sanchez’s moments on the world stage have failed to translate into better living conditions for people in Spain. “You can’t eat GDP,” Feijoo told the prime minister during a televised debate last week.
Critics also say the economic indicators might have indeed improved, but this was mostly driven by the absorption of foreign labour; the minimum wage has increased, but average salaries have remained the same; and services feel increasingly stretched as foreign-born residents have grown by more than four million since the PSOE took power in 2018.
Sanchez’s reputation has also been tarnished by corruption cases involving his inner circle and family, the handling of a migration crisis in the North African enclave of Ceuta earlier this year and two deadly train crashes a few months apart that provided the opposition with ammunition to attack the government for overseeing a failed state that very much needs repairing.
This has energised Vox, which has become a rising political force in recent years. Campaigning on giving Spaniards “national priority” – a system that would create a two-tier society in which Spanish nationals would have better access to social benefits – and banning mass regularisation of migration, the far-right party is predicted to make the biggest gains compared with the other major parties. In 2023, it secured 33 of the 350 seats in Congress; it is now set to double that, capturing about 18 percent of the national vote.
“We’re governed by a criminal mafia, led by an unscrupulous boss who knows no bounds when it comes to lying,” Vox leader Santiago Abascal told supporters at his last rally, held inside a bullring in Valencia, on Friday.
Feijoo has previously said he would prefer the PP to rule on its own, with Vox supporting it in parliament, rather than forming a joint governing coalition. That will depend on numbers: should the far-right party make major gains, it will have stronger leverage in any negotiations.
Yolanda Roman, the global director for public affairs at ATREVIA, said the prospect of a PP-Vox coalition seems to frighten voters less than it did in 2023. That could make it harder for the Socialists to rally voters by warning them about the far right entering government. “I see less fear,” she said, “or maybe we have come to terms with the idea that this is happening.”
The two parties already govern together in four regions, including the former socialist stronghold of Andalusia . Judging by what Vox has demanded of the PP in regional negotiations, Sanchez-Garcia said, a strong result on Sunday could embolden it to ask for key ministries.
Polling stations will open at 9am local time (08:00 GMT) and close at 8pm (19:00 GMT). Official provisional results will start trickling in straight away, with the overall picture expected to be clear before midnight.

Australia's conservatives hope for victory as polls closed on Saturday for Victoria's state election in the region of Melbourne, the country's second-largest city.
The election was set to deal a potential blow to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's centre-left Labor party, which has been ruling the "Garden State" region for 12 years.
Recent opinion polls projected the Labour to be widely ousted by the state Liberal Party leader Jess Wilson, a 36-year-old first-term lawmaker who has vowed to restore fiscal discipline in the deeply indebted state.
If Wilson manages to unseat Labor incumbent Ben Carroll, she would become the first Liberal woman to take office as premier of the state — considered "Australia's toughest job" by the country's business newspaper, the Australian Financial Review.
Her main pledge is to reduce Victoria's debt — the highest in the country — through a total of Aus$20 billion (€12.2 billion) measures, including a controversial plan to privatise the sewerage system.
"I know there are a lot of polls, there are a lot of headlines, but this election is going to be closer than what people think," Wilson told Channel 7, one of Australia's major TV networks.
If Labor loses in Victoria, which is seen as a pacesetting state, it would pile even more pressure on Australia's PM, who has seen his approval ratings tumble to record lows due to discontent with the rising cost of living.
The country's central bank was again forced to raise interest rates to an 18-year high, citing the prolonged war in the Middle East and frequent inflationary pressures.
The far-right anti-immigration One Nation party, led by Pauline Hanson, could pick up some seats in the state's parliament for the first time, according to polls.
Marginalised for years, One Nation has lately become one of Australia's most popular political parties, which could play a kingmaker role in the next Victoria government.
"We know that Labor's out of the state. Finished," Hanson told media, pre-emptively taking credit for Labor's defeat.
"They won't be in government, and that's where One Nation has played a big part in this," she said. "The Liberals could not have won it by themselves. No way in the wide world."

ChatGPT-maker OpenAI has counter-sued Apple, alleging that the iPhone maker stole trade secrets through a former employee.
In a federal lawsuit filed in July, Apple sued the artificial intelligence (AI) company and two of its employees who previously worked for Apple, claiming it had engaged in a "pattern of theft" of proprietary information.
A countersuit, filed in California on Friday, alleged that Apple gained confidential information through the hiring of a former OpenAI employee and accuses it of discouraging hardware suppliers from working on future OpenAI devices.
Apple denied the counterclaims, describing them as "a transparent attempt to distract from the substance" of its own case.
OpenAI is developing AI-enabled personal devices, which it claims in the countersuit could threaten to "outcompete Apple on what Apple views as its own turf".
The filing alleged Apple had gained confidential information by rehiring a former employee who had worked at OpenAI for six months.
OpenAI accused the employee, who it said gained access to information on a new device and the company's roadmap for future physical products, of sending "dozens of OpenAI documents" to his personal phone numbers. It also said he presented OpenAI's plans to senior Apple staff "at Apple's request".
OpenAI said: "Given the timing, it now appears that stealing those documents may have been his reason for joining OpenAI in the first place."
The counterclaim also alleged Apple encourages employees to mix work files with their personal iCloud (Apple's cloud storage service) accounts so it could later accuse those who leave to work for competitors of theft.
A spokesperson for Apple said: "This case is about OpenAI employees deliberately stealing, accessing, and using Apple's secret and confidential information regarding our unreleased technologies, processes, and products - not about inadvertent retention of Apple information."
In its own lawsuit, the tech giant alleged that at least two long-time Apple workers who left the company to join OpenAI took part in a "pattern of theft" by emailing themselves internal Apple information.
Apple also accused the AI firm of undertaking a "strategy to extract Apple's confidential information".
A spokesperson for OpenAI previously denied the claims, telling the BBC: "We have no interest in other companies' trade secrets."
Along with OpenAI, and two former Apple employees, Apple is also suing io Products, the design startup founded by Sir Jony Ive, a long-time Apple executive who designed the iMac, iPod, iPhone and iPad.
OpenAI acquired the company last year in a $6.5bn (£4.7bn) deal.

The Canadian man who sold toxic chemicals through online suicide forums in 40 countries apologised in court to the families of the victims, saying he deeply regrets his actions and will never repeat them.
Kenneth Law made the remarks on Friday during a sentencing hearing where prosecutors asked a judge to give him a 25-year prison term.
The 61-year-old pleaded guilty in May to 14 counts of aiding the suicide deaths of 14 people in Ontario, Canada, though he has admitted to causing the deaths of dozens of victims in England and Wales.
He will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths under a plea deal which saw Canadian authorities withdraw more serious charges of murder.
During Friday's sentencing hearing in an Ontario court, prosecutors stressed that many of his victims were young and struggling with mental distress.
If Law receives the prosecution's recommended sentence, he would serve just under 20 years in prison, after accounting for credit for time served since his May 2023 arrest.
As she sought to make her case in court on Friday, Crown Attorney Kathleen Doherty described Law as a predator taking advantage of "vulnerable people".
"What they needed was help. But what they found was Mr Law and his products for death," Doherty said.
"If people could pay, he sold it to them. There's no discussion or inquiries or anything going on whereby Mr Law would have any ability to appreciate the circumstances of the individual he was dealing with," she said.
Law's defence lawyer, Matthew Gourlay, countered those claims, arguing that his client was not responsible for any of their battles with mental illness..
"Each of these incidents is its own unique tragedy," Gourlay said. "Mr Law may be a common denominator between them, but Mr Law was not the cause of the struggles and hardships that caused all these victims to seek out his products in the first place."
He said Law held a "misguided belief" he was helping his victims
Law's defence attorney has asked the court to give him a 12-year sentence.
At the end of the hearing, Law told the court that he had deep regret for aiding in the suicide deaths of his victims.
"To the families of the victims, words can never replace the loss of your loved ones. I convey my deepest condolences. I remain remorseful. I'm sorry."
The sentencing hearing followed an emotional few days of testimony in September, when grieving family members and friends told the court of the pain Law had caused.
Those impact statements will be taken into account at sentencing, which is due at a later date.
Authorities said the former chef sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients - who he met in online suicide forums - in 40 countries, roughly a quarter of which were sent to the UK.
If you or anyone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this article, details of organisations offering information are available at BBC Action Line

Exclusive: inmate from HMP Manchester now back in custody after 13 hours on the run
A prisoner from one of England and Wales’s most dysfunctional high-security jails is believed to have used soap to help escape from officers while visiting a hospital for treatment.
The 36-year-old detained at HMP Manchester managed to slip away despite being cuffed and chained to an officer, sources told the Guardian. He is believed to have lathered his metal cuff with liquid soap and slipped his hand out while being given privacy to use a bathroom.
After 13 hours of freedom and a short pursuit on foot, the offender was detained and arrested by Greater Manchester police officers.
The incident has sparked a formal inquiry by the Ministry of Justice, and comes amid an increase in escapes from jails in England and Wales.
This is the second time this year that a prisoner has escaped after attending a Manchester hospital.
Marwan Jumaa, a 20-year-old Sudanese national deemed to be a risk to himself and others, was serving an indefinite secure hospital sentence for attacking two women. He escaped after being transferred from his secure hospital facility to North Manchester hospital for medical treatment in July.
Mark Fairhurst, the national chair of the prison officers’ union, the POA, demanded that more officers should escort offenders from category A and B prisons to hospitals.
“This incident highlights the risks that officers face when escorting prisoners to and from hospitals. There should be a minimum of three officers on every hospital appointment instead of two under current rules,” he said.
The number of prisoners escaping from custody has steadily increased over the past three years. In 2025-26, 14 people escaped from custody across England and Wales, compared with 12 the year before, and nine in 2023-24.
HMP Manchester, once known as Strangeways and which houses category A and B prisoners, has been said to have some of the worst conditions across the England and Wales estate.
The category B prisoner escaped on the evening of 20 November after two prison officers accompanied him to a local hospital.
According to prison escort regulations, category B prisoners must wear “double handcuffs” – where both wrists are restrained close to each other and a prisoner is cuffed to a member of staff.
Subject to risk assessment, the double cuff can be adjusted to a single cuff and a ratchet chain when privacy and hand movements are required, such as when using the toilet or shower. This allows the prison officers to give an offender privacy in a room or cubicle while still being attached to an officer via a chain, which can be more than a metre long.
Sources said that the prisoner had been placed in a single cuff and chain but had escaped from his cuff while using a bathroom. Police were alerted at 8.30pm and searched for the man overnight. He was located at 9.30am on Saturday, and was detained and arrested after attempting to flee on foot.
The internal MoJ investigation will focus on whether safety procedures were carried out at all times and if the man was handcuffed properly.
A spokesperson for Greater Manchester police said: “We received a call shortly before 8.30pm on Friday 20 November that a 36-year-old man had absconded from lawful custody whilst at hospital.
“Officers deployed and utilising specialist resources conducted a full search over the course of the evening and into the morning. The man was safely detained at around 9.30am on Saturday 21 November following a short foot chase and further arrested on suspicion of escaping lawful custody. He has been transported back to custody.”
Prison sources said the escape of a prisoner held in a high-security prison was still relatively rare.
In September 2023, Daniel Khalife, 23, sparked a high-profile search when he broke out of HMP Wandsworth by clinging to the underside of a food delivery truck. At the time he was being held on remand for spying charges.
Last year, an escaped prisoner tried to flee armed police by ramming them with his getaway car. Jay Bennett, 33, was serving a nine-year sentence when he absconded from HMP Sudbury in Derbyshire.
An official report into HMP Manchester conducted earlier this year by the prisons watchdog found large quantities of drugs flown in by drones, an obvious rat infestation and violence against prisoners and staff.
The report by Charlie Taylor, HM chief inspector of prisons, said the jail was “in a precarious state”. In 2024, he invoked an urgent notification, which automatically triggers ministers to intervene in the jail’s management.
A Prison Service spokesperson said: “This individual is now back in custody. We have launched an investigation into this incident and any prisoner who is unlawfully at large faces extra time in prison.”

Russia shot down over 1,200 drones targeting Moscow overnight, Russian authorities said Saturday. Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up their attacks using projectiles in recent months, with Ukraine confirming on Friday it had downed a Russian jet-powered drone with laser technology for the first time. Follow our liveblog for the latest updates.
Russian ​forces ​hit a substation in Kyiv ​and ‌a ⁠thermal ‌power station in ⁠the Kyiv region, ​the Russian ‌Defence Ministry said ‌on Saturday.
The ​ministry added that it had ​struck ​a ​vessel carrying military ​cargo in the Black ⁠Sea.
Russian strikes on Ukrainian bridges reached a record high in October-November, following a surge in Ukrainian attacks on Russian bridges, AFP analysis of data from the ACLED conflict monitor shows.
This year, there have been around 40 Russian drone strikes on bridges in Kyiv.
Ukraine has, in turn, staged almost 60 strikes or sabotage operations this year on bridges in territory occupied or annexed by Russia -- 12 times as many as in 2024 or 2025.
Bridges in the Ukrainian capital Kyiv were the prime targets during October-November, according to the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED) NGO.
Since its invasion in 2022, Russia has targeted strategic infrastructure in Ukraine, disrupting supply chains and civilian traffic.
AFP studied ACLED data on daily strikes up to November 20 from sources that include media reports.
At least nine civilians across Ukraine were reported killed on Saturday, while Russia said it had downed a near-record number of Ukrainian drones during the night.
Seven people were killed and seven others wounded in a Russian attack on an enterprise in Nizhyn, in Ukraine's northern Chernihiv region, the State Emergency Service reported on Saturday. It said the rescue operations there finished on Saturday following the attack the previous day.
In Russian-occupied Ukraine, two people died and two others were wounded when a Ukrainian drone struck a hospital vehicle in the southern Zaporizhzhia region, Kremlin-installed authorities there said on Saturday.
“A drone attacked an official vehicle belonging to the Vasylivka Central District Hospital. As a result of the strike, a nurse and a driver were killed. Two others sustained injuries of moderate severity,” the Russian-installed local health ministry said. It added the hospital’s chief physician was among those hurt. The hospital is near the front line.
In a message posted on social media, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that nine Ukrainian children returned on Friday from Russia and Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories.
The Ukrainian president thanked the First Lady of the United States, Melania Trump, for her mediation, as well as the Ukrainian ombudsman and his team.
He added that 2,875 children had been brought back to Ukraine to date.
Ukraine's President ⁠Volodymyr Zelensky said that ​Ukraine's operation that sank a Russian warship ​at a Libyan
naval base had been carried out without prior coordination with European allies.
Zelensky said late on ​Friday ‌that he confirmed this during a ⁠phone call with Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.
"We discussed the ‌issues we are dealing with right now, ⁠and it’s important that we understand each other," Zelenskiy said in a post on X.
"I ​confirmed that the recent operation in ‌Libya was conducted without prior coordination with our European partners."
Meloni has warned Ukraine against allowing the war ‌with Russia, which is in its fifth year after Russia's full-scale invasion ​in February 2022, to spill into the Mediterranean Sea.
Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday unveiled a new nuclear-powered submarine and said Russia would add five more to the country's fleet by 2030, according to footage released by the Kremlin.
At the Sevmash shipyard in the northwestern city of Severodvinsk, Putin attended a flag-raising ceremony aboard the Perm submarine, marking its formal transfer to the navy.
"Russia is one of the few countries in the world capable of building powerful nuclear submarines of this kind, weapons with global reach and significance," he said.
Nuclear-powered submarines are a key part of Russia's nuclear deterrent because their ability to operate covertly underwater ensures a retaliatory strike capability in the event of an attack.
Putin said the navy would receive five more by 2030, including three vessels from the Yasen-M class, the same class as the Perm.
The submarines can operate in "any part of the world's oceans" while carrying a range of cruise missiles, he added.
The ‌governor of Russia's Bryansk region ​said a Ukrainian drone attacked a bus in the village ​of Klimovo – just south of Moscow – overnight, wounding ​nine people.
The ​governor of Samara region said ​Ukraine had made another attempt to attack industrial facilities overnight, adding ⁠that there were no deaths ⁠or ​injuries.
Russian authorities said Saturday that more than 1,200 Ukrainian drones had been shot down in a new night-time attack, with hundreds aimed at the Moscow region.
Ukraine also reported hundreds of Russian drones fired at several regions, with one person killed and five injured.
More than 460 drones headed towards the Moscow area between late Friday and early Saturday, the capital's mayor Sergei Sobyanin wrote on the state-backed Max platform. He added that 123 were destroyed as they neared the city.
The Russian defence ministry said that air defence forces "intercepted and destroyed 1,246 Ukrainian fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles" in more than a dozen regions including Moscow.
Ukraine has for the first time used a laser weapon to shoot down a Russian jet-powered drone, its state-backed defence group Brave1 told AFP on Friday.
Earlier this week, Serhiy Beskrestnov, an adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky, published footage showing a target crashing in a fireball, saying a Russian Geran jet drone had been shot down by a laser system.
The weapon was developed by a recipient of a Brave1 grant and operated by a private air defence team, the Brave1 team confirmed.
But they cautioned that "a first successful interception does not mean the technology is ready for mass deployment".
"Laser air defence remains an experimental technology," the contact said, adding at least seven teams in Ukraine were currently working on laser weapons.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky expressed frustration with the US stance towards Russian leader Vladimir Putin, in the latest sign of deepening tension between Kyiv and Washington, as new questions emerged about Europe’s future financial commitments to Ukraine.
In an interview with the BBC broadcast Friday Zelensky said he wants the US to apply more pressure on Putin to stop his invasion of Ukraine, which began almost five years ago and grinds on despite US President Donald Trump’s efforts to broker a peace deal.

Gösteride, üniversite öğrencileri eğitim koşullarının iyileştirilmesini talep etti.
Binlerce gösterici ilk olarak Tiran'daki İskenderbey Meydanı'nda toplandı, ardından Başbakanlık binasının bulunduğu Ulusun Şehitleri Bulvarı'na yürüdü.

Polis, göstericilerin Başbakanlık binasına yürümelerine izin vermedi.
Yüzlerce polisin görev yaptığı gösteriler nedeniyle bazı yollar trafiğe kapandı.
Başbakan Edi Rama, "diyalog" çağrısında bulunurken, göstericiler bu çağrıyı reddediyor. Öğrenciler protestolarını sürdüreceklerini belirtiyor.

Demonstrations condemning violence against women are set to draw thousands across France on Saturday, with feminist organisations, labour unions, students and Yellow Vest activists expected to take part. The marches come amid a broader wave of social unrest, with cost-of-living protests entering their seventh consecutive week.

Calls to protest gender-based violence across France this Saturday are expected to draw thousands amid the ongoing cost-of-living demonstrations that have continued for almost two months .
“We are calling for a feminist tidal wave to be organised in all our cities, to acknowledge that sexist and sexual violence must stop,” Sophie Binet, general secretary of the France's CGT labour union, told reporters.
The feminist demonstrations come amid a wave of protests across French cities, with students demanding more resources for schools and universities alongside cost-of-living demonstrations entering their seventh consecutive Saturday.
The protests, which have caused multiple clashes with police, appear to be losing momentum. Several hundred thousand people joined marches on the first Saturday of protests on October 17 compared with tens of thousands last week.
Two separate marches against gender-based discrimination are expected to take place in Paris from 2pm, with the police prefecture estimating a turnout of around 40,000 people.
One of the demonstrations, organised by the feminist collective #NousToutes , will march from Place de la République to Place de la Nation to denounce “gender, social, and state violence.” The other, organised by associations and unions brought together as part of the Feminist Strike collective, will mobilise from Place du Panthéon to Place d’Italie to demand “the elimination of violence against women”.
Watch more Violence against women: Its many forms and the paths to justice .
The Yellow Vest movement, mobilised against the cost of living and for more direct democracy , has also called for demonstrations on Saturday against sexist and sexual violence and for gender equality. In Paris, it has arranged to meet at République with #NousToutes .
At the heart of the feminist demands is the adoption of a bill against sexism and sexual violence. Born out of recent feminist protests and placed on the parliamentary agenda after the shockwave caused by the death of schoolgirl Lyhanna in June, the text aims to address the chain of violence against women and children, from prevention to reparation.
The law was adopted by the National Assembly on October 13 and is due to be examined by the Senate in January.
“The goal is for the text to be voted on in time [before the parliamentary session scheduled for February 28, 2027], that it be as ambitious as possible, and that it be given a comprehensive budget,” said Floriane Volt, from the Women's Foundation. The organisation estimates that the bill's implementation will cost €4 billion per year.
Read more France investigates actor Depardieu, writer Houellebecq over alleged gang rape
Last year, demonstrations organised around the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women brought together 17,000 people in Paris and as many across the rest of the country, according to data cited by French police .
More than one hundred femicides took place in France last year, while 272,000 women were victims of rape in 2024, and 1.3 million victims of sexual harassment, according to an official report published on Wednesday.
